orgs.d: A Masonic lodge first chartered in 1877 under the Grand Orient of Italy; Licio Gelli reorganised it from 1970 and became its Venerable Master in 1975. The Grand Orient revoked its charter in 1974, but Gelli kept it running as an unaffiliated lodge. On 17 March 1981 police found a list of 962 names at Gelli's Villa Wanda in Arezzo, including the heads of all three Italian intelligence services (SISMI, SISDE, CESIS), about 195 military and security officers, 44 members of parliament and three ministers, and banker Michele Sindona. Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982 dissolved it, and the Anselmi parliamentary commission reported in 1984. In Argentina, junta member Emilio Massera and minister José López Rega were members.
orgs.cite: Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984; Law 17/1982; Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due'
orgs.reach_src: Countries where P2 had lodges or members, per Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due' (drawing on the Anselmi Commission and later histories).

orgs.d: The senior Grand Lodge of regular Freemasonry, descended from four London lodges that met at the Goose and Gridiron alehouse on 24 June 1717; formally constituted at Freemasons' Hall on 27 December 1813. It has over 200,000 members in more than 6,800 lodges; lodges abroad are grouped into 33 District Grand Lodges and five Groups. In the 1990s Home Secretary Jack Straw required police officers, judges and magistrates who were Freemasons to declare it; in 2009 Straw dropped the rule for judges and magistrates, reportedly over fear of losing at the European Court of Human Rights. The Grand Master since 1967 is Prince Edward, Duke of Kent.
orgs.cite: UK Home Office disclosure rule (1998) and its withdrawal (2009); Wikipedia 'United Grand Lodge of England'
orgs.reach_src: UGLE says it runs 33 overseas District Grand Lodges, but the source used does not name them; only the home jurisdiction is listed as documented.

orgs.d: France's largest Masonic body, formed in 1773 from a split in the older Grand Lodge of France. In 1877, at the urging of pastor Frédéric Desmons, it dropped the requirement to believe in a Supreme Being, and the United Grand Lodge of England and its allies have not recognised it since. Under the Third Republic many Radical and later Socialist politicians were members. In the 1904 Affaire des Fiches it was revealed that the War Ministry had used Grand Orient files on army officers' religious and political views to block Catholics from promotion.
orgs.cite: Affaire des Fiches, Chamber of Deputies debate 1904; Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'
orgs.reach_src: Lodges outside France named in Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'.

orgs.d: France's English-recognised 'regular' Grand Lodge, founded in Paris in 1913 by a lodge that broke from the Grand Orient and an independent lodge in Bordeaux. In December 2009 Grand Master François Stifani faced a revolt over €17 million spent; in January 2011 a court put the Grand Lodge under an appointed administrator. The United Grand Lodge of England suspended relations on 14 September 2011 and withdrew recognition on 12 September 2012, then restored it in June 2014 after Jean-Pierre Servel replaced Stifani. Membership of francophone African heads of state is widely reported but is not documented in the source used here.
orgs.cite: UGLE withdrawal of recognition 2012 and restoration 2014; Wikipedia 'Grande Loge Nationale Française'
orgs.reach_src: The source used gives no list of GLNF lodges abroad; only France is documented.

orgs.d: Italy's main Masonic body, founded in 1805 under the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy. Mussolini suppressed Freemasonry in 1925; it was restarted after the Second World War. It originally chartered the P2 lodge and revoked the charter in 1974. The United Grand Lodge of England withdrew recognition in 1993, citing corruption and Mafia accusations, and restored it in March 2023. In September 2015 it reported 22,675 members in 842 lodges.
orgs.cite: UGLE derecognition 1993 and re-recognition 2023; Wikipedia 'Grand Orient of Italy'
orgs.reach_src: Home jurisdiction; no foreign lodges documented in the source used.

orgs.d: A male, Afrikaner Calvinist secret society founded in 1918 as Jong Zuid Afrika and renamed the Afrikaner Broederbond in 1920, when it had 37 members. Between 1948 and 1994 every South African prime minister and state president was a member. Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom's 1978 book 'The Super-Afrikaners' listed about 7,500 members; other counts run from 6,800 to 12,000 in about 450 branches. Its last chairman, Tom de Beer (1993–94), went on to chair its successor, the Afrikanerbond.
orgs.cite: Wilkins & Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978); Wikipedia 'Afrikaner Broederbond'

orgs.d: A senior society at Yale University founded in December 1832 by William Huntington Russell and Alphonso Taft. It taps 15 juniors a year. Members who reached national office include Presidents William Howard Taft, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush, and Secretary of State John Kerry, who ran against Bush in 2004. It has one chapter and no documented presence abroad.

orgs.hq: San Francisco; camp at Bohemian Grove, Sonoma County
orgs.d: A private men's club formed in San Francisco in April 1872 by journalists; wealthy and powerful men came to control it. Each year it holds a two-week camp at Bohemian Grove in Sonoma County. Members have included several US presidents, usually before election, and many cabinet officers; Richard Nixon was an honorary member. A memo has linked Ronald Reagan's 1983 Social Security cuts to a Bohemian Club meeting in 1981.

A white-supremacist secret order in three waves: 1865–1872, 1915–1944 and from 1946 to today in scattered groups. The second Klan had an estimated 3–6 million members at its 1920s peak. In Indiana it backed Edward Jackson's 1924 win for governor; its Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson led it in 22 northern states until his 1925 murder conviction. Hugo Black gave over 100 speeches to Klan meetings during his 1926 Senate race and was appointed to the US Supreme Court in 1937. Congress passed the Enforcement Acts of 1870–71, including the Ku Klux Klan Act, and President Grant suspended habeas corpus in parts of South Carolina in 1871.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Ku Klux Klan' (Saskatchewan organisers 1926–28 and influence in the provincial Conservative party).

orgs.d: A secret society of Serbian army officers whose constitution was signed on 9 May 1911, organised in cells of three to five, with hundreds of members by 1914. Its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), had led the May 1903 coup in which officers killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade. Apis allegedly ordered the 1914 assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo: three young Bosnian Serbs were recruited, trained and smuggled into Bosnia. Whether Apis was involved, and whether the executive committee approved it, is disputed.

A völkisch occult society that Rudolf von Sebottendorf named at its dedication in Munich on 18 August 1918. It sponsored the German Workers' Party (DAP), founded by Anton Drexler and Karl Harrer in January 1919; Hitler joined that September and it became the NSDAP by February 1920. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke counts Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank as members and Alfred Rosenberg, Dietrich Eckart and Gottfried Feder as guests; there is no evidence Hitler attended. It faded after Hitler cut the party's link in 1920 and dissolved about 1925.
orgs.cite: Goodrick-Clarke, The Occult Roots of Nazism; Wikipedia 'Thule Society'

orgs.d: A Catholic institution founded by Josemaría Escrivá in Madrid on 2 October 1928; its headquarters moved to Rome in 1946. It reported 95,318 members in 2018 (about 85,000 in 2025). Several members, including Alberto Ullastres, served as ministers under Franco; historians Paul Preston and Brian Crozier argue they were picked for skill, not membership. Pope Francis's motu proprio Ad charisma tuendum (in force 4 August 2022) moved its oversight to the Dicastery for the Clergy and barred its prelate from becoming a bishop.
orgs.cite: Opus Dei, 'Regional Circumscriptions of Opus Dei'; Ad charisma tuendum (2022); Wikipedia 'Opus Dei'
orgs.reach_src: Opus Dei's own list of countries in its regional circumscriptions (opusdei.org). Hong Kong, Macau, Puerto Rico and Taiwan are also listed there but are not on the canonical country list; 'Congo' on that list is unspecified.

orgs.hq: Palazzo Malta, Via dei Condotti, Rome
orgs.d: A Catholic lay order descended from the Knights Hospitaller (papal recognition 1113), seated in Rome since 1834, with about 13,500 knights, dames and chaplains. It is a sovereign subject of international law, a UN General Assembly observer since 1994, and has formal diplomatic relations with 114–115 states. In 2016–17 Grand Master Matthew Festing removed Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager over condom distribution in a Myanmar aid project; in January 2017 Pope Francis ordered Boeselager reinstated, required Festing to resign and named Archbishop Giovanni Becciu his special delegate.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Sovereign Military Order of Malta'; 'Foreign relations of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta'
orgs.reach_src: States with full diplomatic relations, per Wikipedia 'Foreign relations of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta' (115 incl. Holy See). National associations exist in other countries (e.g. US, UK, France) but are not listed in the source.

orgs.n: Institute for the Works of Religion (Vatican Bank, IOR)
orgs.d: The Holy See's bank, founded by Pius XII on 27 June 1942. Archbishop Paul Marcinkus ran it from 1971 to 1989; he allegedly issued letters of patronage backing Banco Ambrosiano, which collapsed in 1982 unable to account for $1.287 billion. The IOR denied legal liability but acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to Ambrosiano's creditors. In 2010 Italian magistrates seized €23 million over alleged anti-money-laundering breaches; two former officials were convicted in 2017 and ex-president Angelo Caloia was sentenced for embezzlement in 2021.
orgs.cite: 1984 IOR settlement with Ambrosiano creditors; Vatican tribunal 2021; Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

orgs.hq: Mexico City (founded); general direction in Rome
orgs.d: A Catholic congregation founded by Marcial Maciel in Mexico City on 3 January 1941, part of the Regnum Christi Federation. It runs a network of private schools and universities for Mexico's elite, including the Anáhuac University Network, and its priests serve as chaplains to business leaders in Latin America. The Vatican removed Maciel from ministry in 2006 and in 2010 said his actions were real crimes.
orgs.cite: Holy See communiqués 2006 and 2010; Wikipedia 'Legion of Christ'
orgs.reach_src: Education centres and 2009 apostolic visitation regions named in Wikipedia 'Legion of Christ'.

orgs.d: A Catholic lay movement founded by Fr. Luigi Giussani in Milan in 1954; it says it is present in about 90 countries. Roberto Formigoni, governor of Lombardy and an informal CL political spokesman, was sentenced in December 2016 to six years for bribery and corruption. It runs the annual Rimini Meeting.
orgs.cite: Milan court verdict on Formigoni, 2016; Wikipedia 'Communion and Liberation'
orgs.reach_src: The source gives '90 countries' with no list; only Italy is documented here.

orgs.n: Unification Church / Family Federation for World Peace and Unification
orgs.d: Founded by Sun Myung Moon in Seoul on 1 May 1954; renamed the Family Federation in 1994. Its US arm founded The Washington Times and CAUSA International (New York, 1980), which aided the Nicaraguan Contras. In Japan the Tokyo District Court ordered its religious corporation dissolved on 25 March 2025; the Tokyo High Court upheld it in March 2026 and the Supreme Court confirmed it in June 2026. In South Korea leader Han Hak-ja was arrested in September 2025 and indicted in a special-counsel bribery case linked to former first lady Kim Keon-hee.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court dissolution order 25 Mar 2025; Seoul special counsel indictment Oct 2025; Wikipedia 'Unification Church'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with named activity in Wikipedia 'Unification Church'; the church says it is in about 100 countries.

orgs.d: Under Operation Snow White (1973–77), run by its Guardian's Office (world HQ at Saint Hill Manor, England), agents infiltrated or targeted 136 government agencies, embassies and private bodies in more than 30 countries, including the IRS and Justice Department. After FBI raids on 8 July 1977, eleven senior officials, including Mary Sue Hubbard (five years, $10,000 fine), were convicted in 1979. In Canada the church itself was convicted in 1992 of breach of public trust for infiltrating public offices. France convicted it of organised fraud in 2009.
orgs.cite: United States v. Hubbard (D.D.C. 1979); R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992); Paris criminal court 2009; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Scientology organisations, official inquiries or court cases named in Wikipedia 'Scientology' and 'Operation Snow White'.

orgs.d: An Islamic movement begun by Fethullah Gülen in İzmir in the late 1960s; its first school in Turkey opened in 1982 and by 2010 it ran over 1,000 schools in more than 100 countries. A 17 December 2013 corruption probe by police and prosecutors seen as Gülen-aligned forced four ministers to resign. Turkey designated it a terrorist group in May 2016; after the 15 July 2016 coup attempt over 150,000 officials were dismissed, 2,745 judges were purged by the next morning, and 1,043 schools were shut on 23 July. Turkey's Maarif Foundation said in 2021 it had taken over 216 Gülen-linked schools in 44 countries. Gülen died in Pennsylvania in October 2024.
orgs.cite: Turkish National Security Council designation 2016; Statutory decrees 2016; Maarif Foundation statement 2021 (Turkish Minute); Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Gülen-linked schools named in Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'; Maarif takeover counts from Turkish Minute (2021). 'Congo' in the source is unspecified.

orgs.d: Founded by Hassan al-Banna in Ismailia, Egypt, in March 1928 with six Suez Canal Company workers. Its Freedom and Justice Party won Egypt's presidency in 2012 (Mohamed Morsi), overthrown in 2013; Egypt declared it a terrorist group that December, followed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE in March 2014. Sudan's National Islamic Front took power after the 1989 coup; Hamas began as an offshoot in 1987. Jordan banned the Brotherhood in April 2025. On 13 January 2026 the US named its Lebanese branch a Foreign Terrorist Organization and its Egyptian and Jordanian branches Specially Designated Global Terrorists, citing support for Hamas.
orgs.cite: Egyptian cabinet designation Dec 2013; US State/Treasury designations 13 Jan 2026 (Times of Israel); Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood'
orgs.reach_src: National branches and affiliates named in Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood' and the 2026 US designations. Hamas (Palestine) is not on the canonical country list.

orgs.d: A pan-Islamist party founded in 1953 in Jerusalem by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, aiming to restore a caliphate; it has spread to more than 50 countries. It was allegedly behind failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69 and in Egypt in 1974; a 2004 Nixon Center report cited credible reports of members in coup plots in Jordan, Syria, Egypt, Tunisia and Iraq. It is banned in Bangladesh, China, Russia, Pakistan, India, Germany, Turkey, the UK, Kazakhstan, Indonesia (status revoked July 2017), Australia and all Arab states except Lebanon, Yemen and the UAE.
orgs.cite: National bans; Nixon Center report 2004; Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'
orgs.reach_src: Countries where it operates or has been banned (a ban implies presence), per Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'.

orgs.d: Founded in Tehran in 1953 by the Mashhad cleric Mahmoud Halabi to oppose the Bahá'í Faith; it had about 12,000 members by 1977. Khomeini criticised it on 12 July 1983 and Halabi suspended its activities the same day, though it reportedly revived quietly in the 1990s. People with past ties or sympathies held top posts after 1979, including Ali Khamenei, Ali Akbar Velayati and Mohammad Ali Rajaei; after 1983 members reportedly worked in the judiciary and security services. Former member Ali-Akbar Parvaresh has been implicated, as an allegation, in the 1994 bombing in Buenos Aires.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Hojjatieh' (activity in neighbouring countries by the 1970s, not named).

orgs.d: A Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in Nagpur on 27 September 1925 by K. B. Hedgewar; its 2019 report counted 84,877 branches (shakhas). Two prime ministers, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Narendra Modi, were RSS full-time workers (pracharaks). India banned it after Gandhi's assassination in 1948 (lifted July 1949), during the 1975–77 Emergency, and after the 1992 Babri Masjid demolition. Its overseas arm, the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh, began in Nairobi on 14 January 1947 and says it is active in 156 countries.
orgs.cite: Government of India ban orders 1948, 1975, 1992; Wikipedia 'Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh', 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh'
orgs.reach_src: RSS in India; Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh branches named in Wikipedia 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh' (which claims 156 countries).

orgs.d: A nationalist lobby formed on 30 May 1997 by merging two groups; it claims about 40,000 members in 47 prefectural and about 230 local chapters, and has a parliamentarians' league. After the 2014 reshuffle, 15 of the 19 members of the third Abe cabinet belonged to it, and Shinzo Abe was listed as a 'special adviser'.

A lay Buddhist movement founded on 18 November 1930 by Tsunesaburō Makiguchi and Jōsei Toda. Daisaku Ikeda founded the Komeito party in 1964; it was the Liberal Democratic Party's junior coalition partner from 1999 until the coalition ended in 2025. It claims 8.27 million member households in Japan; scholar Levi McLaughlin estimated under 4 million individuals in 2018. A 1995 French parliamentary report listed it among 173 groups it called cults.
orgs.cite: French National Assembly report on cults 1995; Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'; Soka Gakkai International claims many more countries, not listed in the source.

orgs.d: Founded by Lee Man-hee on 14 March 1984; headquarters in Gwacheon since 1999. In 2020 a Daegu cluster in the church accounted for about 60% of South Korea's COVID-19 cases at one point, and health authorities obtained a list of 317,320 registered members. Lee was arrested on 31 July 2020; in January 2021 he was acquitted of hiding information from contact tracers but convicted of embezzling about 5.6 billion won (four-year suspended sentence), upheld by the Supreme Court in August 2022. China banned the group in 2020 and Singapore charged 21 members.
orgs.cite: Suwon District Court 2021; Supreme Court of Korea 2022; Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus' (the church claims MOUs in 84 countries).

orgs.d: A Christian political network founded by Abraham Vereide in Seattle in April 1935, long led by Doug Coe. It organised the National Prayer Breakfast in Washington from 1953, attended by every president since Eisenhower, until it held a separate event in 2023. Its C Street house in Washington lodged members of Congress, several tied to 2009 scandals (Sen. John Ensign, Gov. Mark Sanford). Journalist Jeff Sharlet tied Fellowship associates to Uganda's proposed death-penalty anti-gay bill; Kremlin agent Maria Butina helped arrange Russian attendance at the 2017 breakfast.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'The Fellowship (Christian organization)'; Sharlet, The Family (2008)

orgs.d: An alleged secret Catholic far-right society said to have been founded in Puebla in the early 1950s; journalist Álvaro Delgado first described it in 2003. Critics allege members in the PAN party and in Vicente Fox's cabinet; named figures, including Governor Juan Manuel Oliva, denied it. In 2014 a Madrid judge said evidence possibly linked members of the Spanish group HazteOír to El Yunque but could not confirm the organisation exists. Nearly all claims come from critics and ex-members.
orgs.cite: Delgado, El Yunque (2003); Madrid court ruling 2014; Wikipedia 'El Yunque (organization)'

orgs.d: A Catholic traditionalist movement founded in Brazil in 1960 by Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; national TFPs followed in about 30 countries. Its campaign against land reform is described as contributing to Brazil's 1964 coup. Chile's Frei government banned the Chilean TFP, which welcomed the 1973 coup; South Africa's P. W. Botha wrote to commend it in 1987; Venezuela's Lusinchi government moved to ban it after an investigation found it operating outside the constitution. Successors include the Heralds of the Gospel (2001) and the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; Poland's Ordo Iuris was founded by a TFP-linked association.
orgs.reach_src: National TFP associations and founding years listed in Wikipedia 'Tradition, Family, Property'.

orgs.n: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture
orgs.d: A Polish Catholic legal think tank founded in 2013 by the Christian Culture Association, which cooperates with the TFP network. In 2016 it drafted a near-total abortion ban that included criminal liability for women; the Sejm rejected it on 6 October 2016 after nationwide 'Black Protests'. In 2021 it helped launch the private university Collegium Intermarium; former PiS education minister Przemysław Czarnek is listed among its supporters. Journalists have documented links to Russian-sponsored ultra-conservative groups.

A Philippine church registered by Felix Manalo on 13 July 1914, with 2.8 million adherents in the 2020 census. It votes as a bloc: in 2016 some INC communities reportedly gave 98–100% of votes to endorsed candidates. It endorsed Benigno Aquino III (2010), Rodrigo Duterte (2016), Bongbong Marcos and Sara Duterte (2022), and its support is cited as one factor in Ferdinand Marcos's 1965 win. Its official directory lists congregations in 72 sovereign states; a 2018 Philippine Senate resolution cited 151 countries and territories.
orgs.cite: Philippine Senate resolution 2018; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo'
orgs.reach_src: The INC directory (72 states) is cited in Wikipedia but not listed there.

orgs.d: A church founded by Apollo Quiboloy in Davao City on 1 September 1985. A US federal grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for child sex trafficking and misuse of donations, and the US Treasury sanctioned him in 2022. In March 2024 its broadcaster SMNI said former President Rodrigo Duterte had been made administrator of its properties. Police raided the Davao compound from 24 August 2024 and arrested Quiboloy in September 2024.
orgs.cite: US v. Quiboloy (C.D. Cal. 2021); US Treasury sanctions 2022; Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Jesus Christ (church)'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia (FBI raids in California, Texas, Hawaii).

orgs.d: A self-help company founded near Albany in 1998 by Keith Raniere and Nancy Salzman, with centres in the US, Canada and Mexico; prosecutors called it a front for crime. Its secret women's group DOS branded members and held 'collateral'. Raniere was convicted in June 2019 and sentenced on 27 October 2020 to 120 years; the Second Circuit upheld it in 2022. Emiliano Salinas, son of former Mexican president Carlos Salinas, and Ana Cristina Fox, daughter of Vicente Fox, have been accused of involvement; NXIVM kept dossiers on officials and pushed officials to investigate critics.

orgs.n: Aum Shinrikyo (now Aleph / Hikari no Wa)
orgs.d: A religious group founded by Shoko Asahara in Tokyo in 1987, growing out of a 1984 yoga school. It recruited members from the Japan Self-Defense Forces and the Tokyo Metropolitan Police. Its sarin attacks killed eight in Matsumoto in 1994 and 14 on the Tokyo subway in 1995. Asahara and 12 others were executed in July 2018. Russia, Japan, Canada, France and the EU designate it a terrorist group; Russia banned it in 2016 and Montenegro expelled 58 linked foreigners that year.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court verdicts; Wikipedia 'Aum Shinrikyo'

orgs.hq: NATO Clandestine Planning Committee (SHAPE) and Allied Clandestine Committee; national HQs e.g. Rome
orgs.d: Secret armed networks set up after 1945 to resist a Soviet invasion, coordinated by NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee (CPC, from about 1949–52) and the Allied Clandestine Committee (ACC, from 1958); per the Belgian inquiry the ACC coordinated networks in ten countries. Italian Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed Gladio to parliament on 24 October 1990, gave a list of 622 members and said 127 arms caches had been dismantled; the last ACC meeting was held 23–24 October 1990. The European Parliament on 22 November 1990 called for all such networks to be dismantled and investigated. Italy, Belgium and Switzerland (P-26) held parliamentary inquiries; Turkey's branch was the Counter-Guerrilla.
orgs.cite: Andreotti statement to the Chamber of Deputies 24 Oct 1990; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990; Belgian and Swiss parliamentary reports 1990–91
orgs.reach_src: National stay-behind networks documented in Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio' (Italy Gladio; Denmark Absalon; Greece LOK/Sheepskin; Turkey Counter-Guerrilla; Switzerland P-26; Austria OeWSGV; France Plan Bleu etc.).

orgs.d: An alleged clandestine 'deep state' network in Turkey prosecuted from 2008 to 2016: 275 defendants, including military officers, journalists and opposition MPs. On 5 August 2013 former Chief of the General Staff İlker Başbuğ was sentenced to aggravated life; 21 defendants were acquitted. In April 2016 the Supreme Court of Appeals annulled all verdicts, finding prosecutors had not proved Ergenekon existed and had collected evidence illegally.
orgs.cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court 2013; Court of Cassation 2016; Wikipedia 'Ergenekon trials'

orgs.hq: Cairo (operations centre); founded at a Kenyan resort
orgs.d: An intelligence alliance chartered on 1 September 1976 by the spy chiefs of France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran, named after the Kenyan resort where it first met; it ran an operations centre in Cairo. Saudi Arabia paid, France supplied technology, and Egypt and Morocco supplied troops and arms. In 1977 French aircraft flew Moroccan and Egyptian troops into Zaire's Shaba province; it armed Somalia in the Ogaden war and gave about $5 million to UNITA in Angola. Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki al-Faisal described it in a 2002 speech at Georgetown.
orgs.cite: Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech 2002; Wikipedia 'Safari Club'
orgs.reach_src: Member intelligence services, per Wikipedia 'Safari Club'.

orgs.d: A cross-border repression system set up at a meeting called by Chile's DINA in Santiago on 25–28 November 1975; Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia signed, Brazil joined in 1976 and Peru and Ecuador later. Members shared intelligence and kidnapped, tortured and killed exiles across borders; John Dinges documented 654 victims from 1976 to 1980. Operations reached Washington (the 1976 Letelier–Moffitt car bomb) and Europe. In 2016 a Buenos Aires court convicted 15 former officers, the first court ruling to recognise Condor.
orgs.cite: Buenos Aires federal court 'Plan Cóndor' verdict 2016; US National Security Archive, 2025 briefing book
orgs.reach_src: Member states per the National Security Archive and Wikipedia 'Operation Condor'.

orgs.n: World Anti-Communist League (now World League for Freedom and Democracy)
orgs.hq: Taipei (HQ); founded as APACL in Jinhae, South Korea
orgs.d: Founded on 15 June 1954 in Jinhae, South Korea, as the Asian Peoples' Anti-Communist League by the Republic of China, the Philippines and South Korea; renamed the World Anti-Communist League in 1966–67 and the World League for Freedom and Democracy from 1991, headquartered in Taipei. Its US chapter, founded by Gen. John Singlaub, and the League were active in aiding the Nicaraguan Contras; after the Iran-Contra scandal, Taiwan's Foreign Ministry confirmed covert Taiwanese aid that League chairman Ku Cheng-kang helped arrange. Participants included Ryōichi Sasakawa, Sun Myung Moon and Paraguay's Alfredo Stroessner; Anderson and Anderson's 1986 book 'Inside the League' documented Nazi collaborators and death-squad figures among members.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'World League for Freedom and Democracy'; 'Iran–Contra affair'; Anderson & Anderson, Inside the League (1986)
orgs.reach_src: Founding states and named national chapters/affiliates (incl. Mexico's Tecos) in Wikipedia 'World League for Freedom and Democracy'. Taiwan (HQ) is not on the canonical country list.

orgs.d: A fake press agency set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's regime, run by ex-OAS captain Yves Guérin-Sérac, with Italian neo-fascist Stefano Delle Chiaie among its founders. It allegedly worked against independence movements in Angola, Mozambique and East Timor. Italian judge Guido Salvini found its instructors trained Avanguardia Nazionale members in explosives and linked it to groups behind the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution its staff fled; a document titled 'Our Political Activity' set out the aim to 'create the conditions favouring the installation of chaos'.
orgs.cite: Investigations of Judge Guido Salvini (Milan); Wikipedia 'Aginter Press'

orgs.n: Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI)
orgs.d: A bank founded in 1972 by Agha Hasan Abedi, registered in Luxembourg with head offices in Karachi and London; within a decade it had over 400 branches in 78 countries. It secretly controlled Washington's First American Bankshares, chaired by former US Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, and handled accounts for Panama's Manuel Noriega. A Luxembourg court ordered it liquidated on 5 July 1991; losses are estimated at $10–17 billion. Senators John Kerry and Hank Brown reported on it to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 1992.
orgs.cite: Kerry–Brown report, 'The BCCI Affair', US Senate 1992; Luxembourg liquidation order 1991
orgs.reach_src: Countries named in Wikipedia 'BCCI' (also Cayman Islands and Hong Kong, not on canonical list). The bank said it operated in 78 countries.

orgs.d: A merchant bank founded in Sydney in 1973 by lawyer Frank Nugan and former US Green Beret Michael Hand, which opened overseas branches and hired retired senior US military and intelligence officers, with former CIA director William Colby as a lawyer. Nugan was found dead near Lithgow in January 1980; Hand destroyed records and fled Australia in June 1980. The 1985 Stewart Royal Commission found banking-law violations and money laundering but no credible evidence of drug smuggling, arms dealing or CIA involvement; the 1980–83 Joint Task Force on Drug Trafficking disputed that.
orgs.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1985; Joint Task Force on Drug Trafficking 1980–83
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Nugan Hand Bank' (branch list not given).

orgs.d: An invitation-only foreign-policy forum founded in 1952–53 by French prime minister Antoine Pinay and intelligence agent Jean Violet, with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss. In 1969 it added Portugal, Spain, Switzerland, the UK and the US; apartheid South Africa sent the only official delegation, and the group backed Renamo and UNITA. Chairmen included Brian Crozier, Julian Amery, Jonathan Aitken, Norman Lamont, and the sitting MPs Rory Stewart and Nadhim Zahawi, who did not declare the role to Parliament. Alan Clark wrote in his diaries that it was CIA-funded.
orgs.reach_src: Founding and 1969 member countries and the South African delegation, per Wikipedia 'Le Cercle'.

orgs.hq: Rotating; first meeting Hotel de Bilderberg, Oosterbeek
orgs.d: An annual private conference first held 29–31 May 1954 at the Hotel de Bilderberg in Oosterbeek, proposed by Józef Retinger and promoted by Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands. Typically 120–150 participants, about two-thirds from Europe and the rest from North America; the 2025 Stockholm meeting had 121 participants from 23 countries, and Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson attended though not on the list. A steering committee has two members from each of about 18 countries. In November 2009 a Bilderberg dinner at Val-Duchesse in Brussels promoted Herman Van Rompuy's candidacy for President of the European Council, which he won.
orgs.reach_src: Host countries of documented meetings and nationalities of chairs/attendees named in Wikipedia 'Bilderberg Meeting' and Polskie Radio (2025). The full 23-country 2025 list was not available.

orgs.d: A private forum founded in 1973 at David Rockefeller's insistence, drawing members from North America, Western Europe and Japan (later Asia-Pacific). In 1980 the Christian Science Monitor counted 21 former members in the Carter administration, including Jimmy Carter, Walter Mondale, Zbigniew Brzezinski and Harold Brown. Its 2022 European and global membership list covered 38 countries.
orgs.cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980; Wikipedia 'List of members of the Trilateral Commission'
orgs.reach_src: Member nationalities in Wikipedia 'List of members of the Trilateral Commission' (Aug 2022 list) plus US and Japan from founding regions.

orgs.hq: Harold Pratt House, 58 East 68th Street, New York
orgs.d: A US foreign-policy membership body incorporated in New York on 29 July 1921, publisher of Foreign Affairs since 1922; 5,397 members in 2025, open only to US citizens and some permanent residents. During the Second World War its Rockefeller-funded War and Peace Studies group wrote 682 confidential memoranda for the State Department. About 40% of top foreign-policy officials under Eisenhower were members; Secretaries of State John Foster Dulles and Cyrus Vance were members.
orgs.reach_src: Offices in New York and Washington only.

orgs.n: World Economic Forum (incl. Young Global Leaders)
orgs.d: Founded by Klaus Schwab on 24 January 1971 as the European Management Forum; renamed in 1987. Its Young Global Leaders programme (begun 1992 as Global Leaders for Tomorrow) has inducted about 1,400 people; alumni who later led governments include Justin Trudeau, Emmanuel Macron, Jacinda Ardern, Sanna Marin, Mark Rutte, Alexander De Croo, Sebastian Kurz and Enrique Peña Nieto. Schwab stepped down as chair on 21 April 2025; an external investigation found no 'material wrongdoing'.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'World Economic Forum', 'Forum of Young Global Leaders'
orgs.reach_src: Headquarters and offices named in Wikipedia 'World Economic Forum' (New York, Beijing, Tokyo, Seoul; C4IR in San Francisco). It also runs 19 Centres for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, not listed in the source.

orgs.d: Founded in Rome in 1968 by Aurelio Peccei and Alexander King; based in Hamburg and, since 1 July 2008, in Winterthur. Its 1972 report 'The Limits to Growth' sold about 30 million copies. Its membership is drawn often from current and former heads of state; honorary members include Mikhail Gorbachev, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, King Juan Carlos I, Horst Köhler, Princess Beatrix and Manmohan Singh. It has national associations in 35 countries and territories.
orgs.reach_src: Founding city and successive HQs; the 35 national associations are not listed in the source.

orgs.hq: Mont Pèlerin, Switzerland (founded); secretariat Lubbock, Texas
orgs.d: A free-market society founded on 10 April 1947 at a meeting Friedrich Hayek organised at Mont Pèlerin above Vevey, with about 39 invited scholars. Members who held top office include President Luigi Einaudi (Italy), Chancellor Ludwig Erhard (West Germany), President Václav Klaus (Czech Republic), Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe (Sri Lanka), Chancellor Geoffrey Howe (UK), finance ministers Carlos Cáceres (Chile) and Ruth Richardson (New Zealand), Secretary of State George Shultz and Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns.
orgs.reach_src: Member countries named in Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

orgs.d: Founded in 1981 by Antony Fisher as the Atlas Economic Research Foundation, it calls itself 'a think tank that creates think tanks'. It grew from 15 think tanks in nine countries in the mid-1980s to 457 in 96 countries in 2020 and 581 members in more than 100 countries in 2024. WNYC reported that partners write legislation and meet policymakers; a 2018 academic article said World Bank Doing Business work 'follows exactly Atlas' policy recommendations'. ALEC is a member.
orgs.reach_src: Countries of partner organisations named in Wikipedia 'Atlas Network' (the full directory covers 100+ countries).

orgs.d: Founded in Chicago in September 1973 as the Conservative Caucus of State Legislators, co-founded by Paul Weyrich. By 2011 it had about 2,000 legislator members, over a quarter of US state legislators, and about 1,000 bills based on its model language were introduced each year, roughly 20% enacted. After Florida's 2005 'Stand Your Ground' law, ALEC adopted it as a model bill and similar laws spread to about 30 states; Coca-Cola and Microsoft left after the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin.

A Chinese Communist Party department, re-established in 1979, that manages relations with non-party groups and overseas Chinese. In January 2022 MI5 issued an alert that London solicitor Christine Lee was suspected of acting for it. A February 2022 Canadian court ruling found its Overseas Chinese Affairs Office engaged in covert intelligence gathering. The US sanctioned its head, You Quan, in January 2021. In 2024 reporters identified 233 people across Europe linked to the united front system, and the Jamestown Foundation found 103 linked groups in Sweden.
orgs.cite: MI5 interference alert Jan 2022; Federal Court of Canada 2022; US sanctions Jan 2021; Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with documented cases in Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'.

orgs.d: A state foundation created by decree of Vladimir Putin on 21 June 2007 to promote Russian language and culture abroad, working with the Russian Orthodox Church. The EU sanctioned it in July 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine. Observers describe it as a tool of Russian soft power and propaganda.
orgs.cite: Presidential decree 21 Jun 2007; EU sanctions July 2022; Wikipedia 'Russkiy Mir Foundation'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Russkiy Mir Foundation' (only the São Paulo centre is named).

orgs.d: The youth and paramilitary wing of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), founded by Col. Alparslan Türkeş in the late 1960s. It was linked to the 1976–80 street violence, including the 1978 Maraş massacre of over 100 Alevis; former prosecutor Emin Değer documented ties to the Counter-Guerrilla, Turkey's Gladio branch. Its second-in-command Abdullah Çatlı died in the 1996 Susurluk crash with a police chief and an MP. Azerbaijan banned it after a 1995 coup attempt, Kazakhstan in 2005 and France in November 2020; since 2018 the MHP has been allied with Erdoğan's AKP.
orgs.cite: Emin Değer; Susurluk parliamentary inquiry 1997; French decree of dissolution Nov 2020
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Grey Wolves (organization)' (presence and bans). Northern Cyprus is not on the canonical list.

orgs.d: An association of current and former soldiers and police set up by André Schmitt, a former soldier of the Bundeswehr's Special Forces Command (KSK) known as 'Hannibal'. Investigators found its chat groups in 2017 while looking into soldiers preparing for a 'Day X' collapse of order. Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classed it internally as a review case by February 2020 and placed it under surveillance in early July 2020. Schmitt was fined under the explosives law after training grenades, smoke cartridges and fuses were found on him.
orgs.reach_src: German authorities' classification and AP reporting.

orgs.d: Anti-communist cultural organisation founded at a West Berlin conference in June 1950 and run from Paris by Michael Josselson. At its height it had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter, Preuves, Quadrant and Transition. Its funding came from the CIA's International Organizations Division until the 1966-67 disclosures; it was then renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom, funded by the Ford Foundation, and dissolved in 1979.
orgs.cite: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence; Saturday Evening Post (Braden), May 1967
orgs.reach_src: Offices, magazines and conferences listed in CCF/IACF publication lists (Bombay 1951, Rangoon, Mexico City, Tokyo, Ibadan, Copenhagen office 1960, Quadrant in Australia, Transition in Uganda)

orgs.n: Asia Foundation (formerly Committee for a Free Asia)
orgs.d: Grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia, created in 1951, and incorporated in California in 1954. A 1966 CIA memorandum calls it a CIA proprietary set up to do cultural and educational work for the US government 'in ways not open to official U.S. agencies'; the project code name was DTPILLAR. After 1967 it was kept and funded openly by the US government, and it now runs governance and development programmes across Asia.
orgs.reach_src: CIA memorandum (programme countries not listed in the memo)

orgs.d: Confederation of US college student governments, founded at the University of Wisconsin in 1947. From the early 1950s to 1967 its international programme was secretly paid for by the CIA, and it helped build anti-communist international student bodies. Ramparts exposed the funding in February 1967; the NSA cut its CIA ties in August 1967 and merged into the United States Student Association in 1978.
orgs.cite: Ramparts, Feb 1967; Church Committee Book I (1976)

orgs.d: Created by the American Federation of Labor at its 1944 convention, with $1 million, and run by Jay Lovestone; Irving Brown was its man in Paris. It funded Force Ouvrière in France from 1948, the Italian CISL, and anti-communist dockworker groups in French, Italian and Greek ports. Historian Anthony Carew found it carried CIA money for about 20 years starting with the 1948 Italian election.
orgs.cite: Anthony Carew, Labor History (1998); Ted Morgan, A Covert Life (1999)

orgs.n: American Institute for Free Labor Development
orgs.d: Chartered in August 1962 by the AFL-CIO with business and government partners under the Alliance for Progress, and funded by contracts with USAID. It trained Latin American union leaders in their own countries and in the United States. Its director William Doherty Jr. said its Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the 1964 coup. In the mid-1990s it was merged into the American Center for International Labor Solidarity.
orgs.cite: Cliff Welch, Latin American Research Review

orgs.d: Anti-communist institute linked to the CIA and financed by multinational companies. It paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in Brazil's October 1962 elections. A parliamentary inquiry commission investigated it and President Goulart closed it in 1963; in 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted US funding of the opposition in that election.
orgs.cite: Brazilian CPI on IBAD (1963); Lincoln Gordon (1977)

orgs.d: Radio Free Europe was launched in 1949 by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front formed by Allen Dulles; Radio Liberty began in 1951. Both took covert CIA money until 1971-72, then open congressional funding through the Board for International Broadcasting from 1974; they merged in 1976 and moved from Munich to Prague in 1995.
orgs.cite: US Congress (Case bill, 1971); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

orgs.n: CIA conduit foundations and front groups (International Organizations Division)
orgs.d: The CIA division headed by Thomas Braden from 1950 handled labour, youth, student and cultural programmes. The Church Committee found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants by 164 US foundations in 1963-66, and nearly half of their international grants. The 1967 Katzenbach Committee ended covert funding of US educational and private voluntary groups.
orgs.cite: Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), pp. 182-192

orgs.d: Private non-profit created by Congress in November 1983 and funded almost wholly by annual congressional appropriations. It gives grants directly and through four core institutes (the party institutes NDI and IRI, the Chamber of Commerce's CIPE and the AFL-CIO's Solidarity Center). Its founder Allen Weinstein said in 1991 that much of its work 'was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA'. Russia banned it as 'undesirable' in 2015 and China sanctioned it in 2019.
orgs.reach_src: Lindsey O'Rourke (Reagan-era NED programmes); LeoGrande (Nicaragua); The Intercept (Venezuela grants); Irving Brown/UNI grants (France, 1980s)

orgs.d: Boston engineering firm founded in 1893, known for hydroelectric and water-resource work abroad, such as Turkey's Sarıyar Dam in the 1950s and a plan for the Jordan River valley. It also sold economic forecasts and feasibility studies. Parsons Corporation bought it in 1985. Its former chief economist John Perkins describes it as a vehicle for loading countries with debt; that account is his own.

orgs.n: US-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation
orgs.d: Bilateral commission set up in 1974 after the oil embargo, co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Finance Minister. The GAO found in 1979 that US technical help under it was paid almost entirely from a Saudi trust account held in the US Treasury, so it ran outside the normal congressional appropriations. It placed US experts in Saudi ministries and agencies on infrastructure and planning projects.

Large US private foundation. It paid for University of Indonesia economists to train at Berkeley from the late 1950s; they became Suharto's economic ministers. It funded the second phase (1965-73) of the University of Chicago-Catholic University of Chile programme, and took over funding of the Congress for Cultural Freedom's successor after 1967.

orgs.n: University of Chicago - Catholic University of Chile programme ('Chile Project')
orgs.d: US government Point Four aid scheme set up in the mid-1950s to link the University of Chicago economics department with Santiago's Catholic University. Between 1955 and 1973, 126 Chilean students trained under it, paid by US aid (to 1964) and then the Ford Foundation. Its graduates wrote 'El ladrillo' and held Pinochet's finance, economy and central bank posts from 1975.
orgs.cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998)

orgs.d: Intergovernmental police organisation of 196 member countries, headquartered in Lyon. Article 3 of its constitution bans activity of a political, military, religious or racial character. Its Red Notices are requests to locate and provisionally arrest; the Commission for the Control of Interpol's Files reviews challenges, and since 2015 a refugee policy bars notices sought by the country a refugee fled. Member governments including Turkey, Russia, China, the UAE and Bahrain have been documented using notices against critics.

UN specialised agency for health. A 2000 committee of experts chaired by Thomas Zeltner found tobacco companies had run a long, well-funded effort to undermine its tobacco-control work. In 2010 the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly criticised its H1N1 decisions for lack of transparency about industry ties.

World football federation. In May 2015 the US Justice Department indicted 14 people, and later dozens more, for bribery tied to marketing rights and World Cup votes; seven FIFA officials were arrested at Zurich's Baur au Lac hotel on 27 May 2015. Several defendants had held public office: a former President of Honduras, a former governor of São Paulo, a Trinidad cabinet minister and a Guatemalan judge.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press releases, 27 May and 3 Dec 2015
orgs.reach_src: FIFA case defendants who held public office

orgs.d: Governing body of the Olympic movement, which chooses host cities by members' vote. In 1999 it expelled ten members and sanctioned ten over gifts from the Salt Lake City bid. Brazilian courts convicted Rio 2016 bid chief Carlos Nuzman in 2021 of buying IOC votes, after Rio governor Sérgio Cabral admitted paying $2 million to IOC member Lamine Diack.
orgs.cite: IOC ad hoc commission (1999); 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio (2021)

orgs.n: Rhodes's secret society ('Society of the Elect') / Milner Group, as described by Carroll Quigley
orgs.d: Carroll Quigley wrote that Cecil Rhodes, W. T. Stead and Reginald Brett (Lord Esher) organised a secret society in London in February 1891, with Rhodes as leader, a 'Junta of Three' (Stead, Brett, Milner), an inner 'Society of the Elect' and an outer 'Association of Helpers'. Rhodes's first will (1877) left his fortune to found a society for 'the extension of British rule throughout the world' and 'the ultimate recovery of the United States'; Quigley says the society appears in five of Rhodes's seven wills. Quigley gives the leaders as Rhodes (to 1902), Milner (to 1925), Kerr or Curtis, then Brand (to 1963) and Adam Marris. The existence of the society as an organisation rests on Quigley; Sir Ivison Macadam of the Round Table called him 'crazy'.
orgs.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written c. 1949, published 1981), ch. 1 and 3; Tragedy and Hope (1966), pp. 950–952
orgs.reach_src: Countries where Quigley places its members in office; membership itself rests on Quigley

orgs.d: Set up under Cecil Rhodes's last will on his death in March 1902 to fund scholarships at Oxford, originally for men from the Commonwealth, Germany and the United States; women were admitted from 1977. Rhodes's purpose was to promote unity among English-speaking nations. The first trustees included Milner, Rosebery, Earl Grey, Alfred Beit and Rhodes's solicitor B. F. Hawksley; Philip Kerr was General Secretary 1925–39. Eight former scholars became heads of state or government, including Bill Clinton, John Turner, Bob Hawke, Tony Abbott and Malcolm Turnbull.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Rhodes Scholarship'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 3
orgs.reach_src: Original eligibility and scholar heads of government (Wikipedia); trust founded from Rhodes's South African fortune

orgs.d: Young Oxford graduates recruited by Alfred Milner from 1901 to staff the colonial government of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony after the Boer War: among them Lionel Curtis, Philip Kerr, Robert Brand, Geoffrey Dawson, Patrick Duncan, Richard Feetham, Lionel Hichens, John Dove, Dougal Malcolm, Hugh Wyndham and Peter Perry. They promoted union of the four colonies, achieved in 1910. On returning to England in 1909 the group renamed itself the Round Table.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

orgs.d: Launched at Plas Newydd, Wales, on 4–6 September 1909 from Milner's Kindergarten, with Lionel Curtis as organiser and Philip Kerr as secretary; its quarterly The Round Table first appeared in November 1910, funded mainly by Abe Bailey and the Rhodes Trust, and is still published as The Round Table: The Commonwealth Journal of International Affairs. Curtis toured the dominions in 1910–11 to set up groups in Canada, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand; a Newfoundland group followed in 1912. Quigley says by 1915 there were groups in seven countries including India and a loose US group (George Louis Beer, Walter Lippmann, Thomas Lamont and others) and calls the movement the outer ring of Rhodes's society.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Round Table movement'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

orgs.n: Royal Institute of International Affairs (Chatham House)
orgs.d: Proposed at a meeting of about 30 British and American peace-conference experts that Lionel Curtis convened at the Hotel Majestic, Paris, on 30 May 1919; inaugurated as the British Institute of International Affairs on 5 July 1920 and given a royal charter in 1926. Canadian donors Reuben and Kate Leonard bought it 10 St James's Square. Its wartime Foreign Research and Press Service under Arnold Toynbee was moved into the Foreign Office in 1943–46. Quigley says Thomas Lamont of J. P. Morgan gave £2,000 for its history of the peace conference and that each dominion institute was formed around the local Round Table group.
orgs.cite: Chatham House, 'The Hotel Majestic and the Origins of Chatham House' (2019); Wikipedia 'Chatham House'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10

orgs.d: Founded in 1925 with a first conference in Honolulu that summer, with national councils in Pacific Rim countries and a secretariat that moved to New York in the early 1930s under Edward C. Carter; funded mainly by the Rockefeller Foundation and the Carnegie bodies. Conferences were held at Kyoto (1929), Shanghai (1931), Banff (1933) and Yosemite (1936). The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee reported in 1952 that it had been 'a vehicle used by the Communists'; the IRS revoked its tax exemption in 1955 but lost in court in 1959, and it dissolved in 1960. Quigley says its British and dominion councils merged with the local institutes of international affairs by 1939.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10
orgs.reach_src: Senate Internal Security Subcommittee 1952 (State Department policy)

orgs.d: Anglo-American dining society founded in London on 16 July 1902 by Sir Harry Brittain; the US society first met at the Waldorf Astoria, New York, on 13 January 1903. It welcomes each new US ambassador to Britain, and US ambassadors in London and secretaries of state are customarily admitted ex officio; the two societies share membership. Churchill spoke to it as Prime Minister on 18 March 1941.
orgs.reach_src: Ex officio membership of US ambassadors and secretaries of state

orgs.d: Russian private military company financed by Yevgeny Prigozhin and used by the Russian state to place fighters, bodyguards and advisers with governments in Syria and Africa, paid partly in mining and timber concessions. Its African structures included M Invest/Meroe Gold (Sudan) and Lobaye Invest (CAR). After Prigozhin's mutiny and death in 2023 most African operations moved to the defence ministry's Africa Corps; Wagner announced its exit from Mali on 6 June 2025, while a reorganised Wagner presence is reported in the CAR.
orgs.cite: US Treasury designations 2020–2023; UN Panel of Experts on Libya (2020); Wikipedia
orgs.reach_src: UN Panel on Libya; US Treasury; Wikipedia country articles

orgs.d: Paramilitary formation of Russia's defence ministry that took over and rebranded most of Wagner's African operations from late 2023. It provides troops, regime protection and training to governments that have expelled French or US forces. Estimated deployments: Mali about 1,000–2,000, CAR 1,500–2,000, Libya 800–1,800, Burkina Faso about 300, Niger 100–300, Equatorial Guinea about 200.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia, citing CTC Sentinel, ISPI, BBC, Al Jazeera

orgs.n: Prigozhin political-technologist and disinformation network (incl. AFRIC)
orgs.d: Teams of Russian political strategists, social-media operators and front bodies funded through Yevgeny Prigozhin's companies, active in African elections from 2018. Facebook removed three of its networks targeting eight African states in October 2019. Its fronts included AFRIC (Association for Free Research and International Cooperation), which sent 'observers' to elections such as Zimbabwe 2018.
orgs.cite: Facebook takedown 30 Oct 2019; Stanford Internet Observatory; Proekt/BBC (2019); EPDE (2020)
orgs.reach_src: Facebook Oct 2019 announcement; EPDE AFRIC report

orgs.d: Party cadre school in Kibaha, Tanzania, built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School and taught partly by CCP instructors. It is run jointly by the CCP and six southern African ruling or former liberation parties. The ANC says it had trained over 1,405 participants by January 2024.
orgs.cite: Africa Center for Strategic Studies (2022); ANC statement (23 Jan 2024)

orgs.d: Shia Islamist party and armed movement in Lebanon, aligned with Iran's Revolutionary Guards and part of the 'Axis of Resistance'. It sits in parliament (about 14 of 128 seats) and in cabinet, while its armed wing is listed as terrorist by at least 28 countries. Since August 2025 the Lebanese cabinet has backed an army plan to disarm it.

orgs.n: IRGC Quds Force and allied militia network
orgs.d: The Quds Force is the external branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which the US listed as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in April 2019. It arms, trains and directs allied groups, several of which sit inside other states' security forces, notably Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces. Courts in several countries have convicted people described as its operatives.
orgs.cite: US State Department FTO listing (2019); Wikipedia

orgs.d: Network of companies owned by brothers Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta and associate Salim Essa, built around Sahara Computers and Oakbay Investments and close to President Jacob Zuma. The Zondo Commission found ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly on its behalf; the US sanctioned the brothers in 2019 and the UK in 2021. The brothers have lived in Dubai since 2016.

US management consultancy. In South Africa it won Eskom and Transnet contracts alongside Gupta-linked Trillian, repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet, and in 2024 paid a $122 million US penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement for bribing South African officials in 2012–2016.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice (2024); Zondo Commission

orgs.d: London public relations firm that ran a paid campaign for the Gupta-owned Oakbay Investments in 2016–17 using fake social-media accounts and 'white monopoly capital' messaging. Expelled by the PRCA on 4 September 2017; went into administration on 12 September 2017.

China's largest telecoms equipment maker, supplier of 'safe city' surveillance and network systems to many African governments. The Wall Street Journal reported in 2019 that its technicians helped Uganda's police and Zambia's government spy on opponents; Huawei denied it. Huawei also equipped the African Union headquarters network found sending data to Shanghai, which it denied.

Israeli maker of Pegasus phone-hacking spyware, sold only to governments under Israeli export licences. Investigations tied state clients including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco, Rwanda and Togo to surveillance of journalists, dissidents and foreign officials. Added to the US Entity List in November 2021.
orgs.cite: US Commerce Department (2021); Citizen Lab; Pegasus Project

orgs.d: Israeli private hacking and disinformation outfit led by Tal Hanan, exposed in February 2023 by the Forbidden Stories 'Story Killers' consortium. Hanan claimed to have worked on 33 presidential elections, many in Africa, and worked with Cambridge Analytica in Nigeria in 2015.
Israeli political consulting firm banned from Facebook in May 2019 for coordinated fake accounts aimed mainly at African elections, after spending about $1.1 million on ads.
orgs.reach_src: Facebook takedown report as reported by CNN and DFRLab

orgs.d: British political data and influence firms. Cambridge Analytica worked on Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 Kenyan campaigns and, with Team Jorge, on Nigeria's 2015 election; executives claimed work on over 200 elections. Both firms closed in 2018 after the Facebook data scandal.

A conservative think tank in Washington. It organised Project 2025, a 900-plus-page governing plan for a conservative administration written with dozens of partner groups. Several of the plan's authors and contributors, including Russ Vought (OMB) and Brendan Carr (FCC), took senior posts in the second Trump administration in 2025.

A Washington think tank founded by John Podesta on 24 October 2003 as a Democratic counterpart to the Heritage Foundation and the American Enterprise Institute. Its staff moved into the Obama and Biden administrations; Business Insider counted nearly 70 former CAP employees in Biden-administration posts by mid-2021. Neera Tanden leads it.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Center for American Progress'; Fox News, 15 September 2022

orgs.n: Federalist Society for Law and Public Policy Studies
orgs.d: A network of conservative and libertarian lawyers and law students formed in April 1982 at Yale, Harvard and Chicago law schools, with about 70,000 members. It helped draw up Trump's 2016 Supreme Court shortlist, and 43 of his first 51 appeals-court nominees were members. The liberal American Constitution Society was founded in 2001 as its counterpart.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Federalist Society'; New York Times, 16 March 2020

orgs.d: A registered cross-party caucus in Brazil's National Congress for evangelical causes. Its vice-president said in February 2023 that 132 deputies and 14 senators had signed on; Agência Pública counted 93 deputies tied to evangelical churches, led by the Assemblies of God, Baptists and the Universal Church.

orgs.n: Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International
orgs.d: A Pentecostal church founded in Colombia. The MIRA political party, founded in 2000, lists it as its religion and holds seats in Colombia's Senate, House and local councils.

Chinese-language and culture centres placed inside foreign universities and schools, funded through China's education ministry (formerly via Hanban). The National Association of Scholars counted about 550 worldwide in 2020. The US State Department designated their US centre a foreign mission of China on 13 August 2020, and 104 of 118 US institutes had closed by June 2022.

A Catholic lay movement founded in October 1914 by priest Josef Kentenich at Schoenstatt near Vallendar, Germany. It is active in more than 100 countries and every Latin American country, with nearly 80 shrines in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. Chile's President José Antonio Kast was raised in it; his brother Miguel Kast was Pinochet's planning minister and Central Bank president.

A transnational criminal organisation operating mainly out of India and led by Lawrence Bishnoi. Canadian officials said in October 2024 that targets identified through Indian diplomats were attacked by the gang. Canada listed it as a terrorist entity on 29 September 2025.

POGOs were online gambling firms licensed by the Philippine gaming regulator PAGCOR, mostly Chinese-owned and serving players in China, where gambling is illegal. They expanded from 2016 under President Duterte; by 2024 PAGCOR counted 48,883 workers. 2024 Senate hearings linked many hubs to fraud, trafficking, torture and fake Filipino identities, including that of Bamban mayor Alice Guo. President Marcos ordered all to close by 31 December 2024 and Congress banned them by law in October 2025.
orgs.cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025)

orgs.d: Conglomerate founded in 2015 by Chen Zhi, a Fujian-born businessman who became a Cambodian citizen and adviser to Hun Sen. It ran property, banking and tourism businesses from Sihanoukville and Phnom Penh. On 14 October 2025 the US indicted Chen for running forced-labour scam compounds and seized about 127,271 bitcoin, while the US and UK sanctioned 146 linked people and firms; Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong also seized assets. Cambodia sent Chen to China in January 2026.
orgs.cite: US DOJ indictment and OFAC/UK sanctions, 14 October 2025
orgs.reach_src: US/UK sanctions and asset seizures as summarised on Wikipedia

orgs.d: Cambodian financial group whose units include Huione Pay (payments), Huione Guarantee (an escrow marketplace on Telegram) and a crypto exchange. Hun To, cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, is a major shareholder and director of Huione Pay. Cambodia's central bank revoked Huione Pay's banking licence in March 2025, and in May 2025 the US Treasury's FinCEN found the group a primary money laundering concern that moved over US$4 billion in illicit funds from 2021 to 2025.

orgs.n: Ma Ba Tha (Association for the Protection of Race and Religion)
orgs.d: Buddhist nationalist monks' organisation formed in January 2014, linked to the 969 movement and the monk Wirathu. Its members proposed the texts of four Race and Religion Protection Laws that Parliament passed in 2015. The state clergy council ordered it disbanded in May 2017; it continued under new names, and its figures have received donations and honours from military leaders.
orgs.cite: Human Rights Watch 2014; State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee order, May 2017

orgs.d: Sinhala Buddhist nationalist organisation of monks founded in 2012, led by general secretary Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara. Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa opened its training centre in 2013, and as president in 2021 appointed Gnanasara to chair a 'One Country, One Law' task force. Gnanasara has been jailed several times; in 2026 the Supreme Court voided his 2019 presidential pardon and he was returned to prison.
orgs.cite: Daily FT, 27 October 2021; Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026

orgs.hq: Nairobi (first branch); national bodies in each country
orgs.d: Overseas counterpart of India's RSS, started as a branch in Nairobi on 14 January 1947 by RSS volunteers; it says it is active in 156 countries with about 3,289 branches. The UK branch dates from 1966; the Charity Commission for England and Wales investigated it after a 2015 ITV programme and in 2016 found trustee mismanagement but no evidence of formal links to the RSS. The RSS said in 2014 the two work closely together but are separate. No case of HSS reaching into a government was found.
orgs.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, inquiry report, 2 September 2016

orgs.d: Pro-democracy party founded in 1982 by Vietnamese exiles, with members in the diaspora and inside Vietnam. Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation on 4 October 2016; rights groups and the US government dispute the label. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership.
orgs.cite: Vietnam Ministry of Public Security, 4 October 2016

orgs.d: A Brussels non-profit set up by former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri to campaign against impunity for human-rights crimes. Belgian investigators say it served as the channel for cash from Qatar, Morocco and Mauritania to influence the European Parliament; its office was raided on 9 December 2022 and about €600,000 in cash was found at Panzeri's home. Panzeri agreed a plea deal in January 2023. Its largest declared donor was a foundation of South African businessman Iqbal Survé.
orgs.cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; Qatargate case file reported by Der Spiegel and Financial Times
orgs.reach_src: Belgian investigation as reported (suspects' nationalities and paying states)

orgs.d: Unofficial offices abroad linked to the public security bureaus of Chinese cities such as Fuzhou, Qingtian, Nantong and Wenzhou. Safeguard Defenders reported in September and December 2022 that they were used to pressure people wanted by China, including dissidents, to return; China says they renew documents and fight fraud. Ireland and the Netherlands ordered stations closed in 2022, the UK said in 2023 they had closed, and US prosecutors charged two men in 2023 over a station in Manhattan (one pleaded guilty in 2024, one was convicted in 2026).
orgs.cite: Safeguard Defenders reports 'Patrol and Persuade' and '110 Overseas', 2022; government statements of Ireland, Netherlands, UK, US
orgs.reach_src: Safeguard Defenders 2022 list as reproduced on Wikipedia, plus governments that announced investigations (Spain, Portugal, Canada)

orgs.d: The name given by the European Stability Initiative in 2012 to Azerbaijan's system of gifts, paid trips and cash for European politicians, especially members of the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly (PACE). A PACE investigation body reported in April 2018 on breaches by members from several countries; an Italian court jailed former PACE group leader Luca Volontè in 2021; the Bundestag lifted two members' immunity in 2021. The Azerbaijani Laundromat leak (2017) showed $2.9 billion moved through Danske Bank Estonia in 2012–2014, part of it to politicians.
orgs.cite: European Stability Initiative reports 2012 and 2016; PACE Independent Investigation Body report, 2018; OCCRP 2017
orgs.reach_src: PACE investigation body report 2018 and OCCRP laundromat recipients

orgs.n: United Russia party – foreign party cooperation agreements
orgs.d: United Russia is Vladimir Putin's ruling party. It signs formal cooperation agreements with foreign parties covering delegation exchanges, contacts between legislators and economic cooperation: Austria's FPÖ signed one on 19 December 2016 (expired end 2021) and Italy's Lega on 6 March 2017 (renewing automatically every five years). Bulgaria's Russophiles party signed a memorandum with it for the 2021 elections.
orgs.cite: Agreement texts published by Il Foglio (Lega) and reported by Vindobona (FPÖ)

orgs.d: A Milan cultural association promoting ties with Russia, presided over by Gianluca Savoini, a long-time aide of Lega leader Matteo Salvini. Savoini was recorded at Moscow's Metropol hotel in October 2018 negotiating an oil deal meant to finance the Lega; Milan prosecutors investigated, and a judge closed the case in April 2023, finding the aim was illicit party financing but the deal never got far enough to be a crime.
orgs.cite: Milan preliminary-investigations judge, dismissal order of April 2023

orgs.n: First Czech Russian Bank (Pervyi Chekhoslovatsko-Rossiiskii Bank)
orgs.d: A Moscow bank that lent €9 million to France's Front National in 2014, confirmed by Marine Le Pen in November 2014. Party officials told Mediapart it was the first part of a €40 million facility.
orgs.cite: Marine Le Pen statement, November 2014; Mediapart

orgs.d: A Russian state think tank. Bulgarian prosecutors charged pro-Russia activist and former MP Nikolay Malinov in 2019 with collecting state secrets for it from 2013 to 2019; a Sofia court acquitted him in May 2026.
orgs.cite: Bulgarian Specialised Prosecution Office, 2019; Sofia court, May 2026

orgs.n: DITIB – Turkish-Islamic Union for Religious Affairs
orgs.d: Founded in 1984 as the German branch of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet; it runs about 900 mosques in Germany. Its imams are trained in Ankara and paid as Turkish civil servants. German federal prosecutors investigated imams in 2017 for spying on Gülen supporters (case dropped in December 2017), and Germany's interior ministry cut its funding in 2018.
orgs.cite: German Federal Prosecutor's Office 2017; Federal Ministry of the Interior 2018

orgs.d: A Shia religious centre founded by Iranian residents of Hamburg in the 1950s and seen as aligned with Iran's government. Germany expelled its deputy director in 2022 over Hezbollah ties and banned the centre in July 2024 as unconstitutional, taking over its mosque building.
orgs.cite: German Federal Ministry of the Interior ban order, July 2024

orgs.d: Pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk, exchanged to Russia in 2022, directed paid influence work in Europe. Czech intelligence exposed the Prague-based site Voice of Europe in March 2024 as run for him by Artem Marchevskyi, paying European politicians; the EU sanctioned it in May 2024. In the UK, former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed in 2025 for taking bribes in 2018–2019 from Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn, who passed on Medvedchuk's requests.
orgs.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; EU Council sanctions May 2024; Old Bailey sentencing remarks, 21 November 2025
orgs.reach_src: Voice of Europe exposure 2024 (Czech, Belgian and Polish investigations; German politicians investigated) and the Gill case

orgs.n: Ilan Shor network (Șor Party and successors)
orgs.d: Moldovan party built around businessman Ilan Shor and backed by Russia. The Constitutional Court declared it unconstitutional on 19 June 2023. Its vice-president Marina Tauber was sentenced to 7½ years in 2025 for illegal party financing, and its Gagauzia governor Evghenia Guțul to 7 years in August 2025 for using undeclared Russian money.
orgs.cite: Constitutional Court of Moldova 2023; Moldovan court sentences 2025

orgs.n: China Association for International Friendly Contact (CAIFC)
orgs.d: A Beijing 'friendship' association. Ye Jianming, chairman of CEFC China Energy, was its deputy secretary-general in 2003–2005 before becoming an economic adviser to Czech President Miloš Zeman; Ye was detained in China in 2018.
orgs.cite: Czech Presidential Office; Reuters reporting on CEFC

orgs.n: Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC)
orgs.d: The four largest audit and advisory networks, called the 'Big Four' since Arthur Andersen collapsed in 2002. They audit most large companies and also sell tax and consulting work to governments, sometimes lending staff to ministries. Cases include the PwC Australia tax leak (2023), KPMG's withdrawn SARS report in South Africa (2017), and the UK Public Accounts Committee's 2013 criticism of staff seconded to the Treasury.
orgs.cite: Australian Senate inquiry 2023; UK Public Accounts Committee 2013

orgs.d: US management-consulting firm founded in Boston in 1973. South Africa's Zondo Commission found it worked with President Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to restructure and weaken the tax service; the UK barred it from government contracts in 2022 (lifted 2023) and South Africa suspended it from state work.

US ride-hailing company. The leaked 'Uber Files' (2022) covering 2013–2017 show it lobbied heads of government and ministers across Europe and beyond while operating in breach of local taxi laws, including help from French economy minister Emmanuel Macron and former EU commissioner Neelie Kroes.
orgs.cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, Uber Files, July 2022

orgs.d: US pharmaceutical company. Its CEO Albert Bourla negotiated the EU's largest Covid-19 vaccine contract partly by text with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen; the EU General Court ruled in May 2025 that the Commission wrongly refused access to the texts.

Supply-chain finance firm founded by Lex Greensill, who earlier held a UK Cabinet Office adviser role. It employed former Prime Minister David Cameron, who lobbied ministers for it in 2020. It collapsed in March 2021.

Brazilian construction and engineering group, renamed Novonor in 2020. In December 2016 it admitted to US, Brazilian and Swiss authorities paying $788 million in bribes in 12 countries through its 'Structured Operations Division', and paid a record fine. The case led to convictions of presidents and ministers in Peru, Ecuador and elsewhere.
orgs.reach_src: US DOJ statement of facts (Wikipedia summary)

orgs.d: Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group owned by Iskandar Safa (died 2024). It supplied boats under Mozambique's $2 billion hidden-debt deals; US prosecutors said it paid Finance Minister Manuel Chang $7 million, and London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from Safa's estate and companies.
orgs.cite: US v. Chang (E.D.N.Y.) 2024; UK High Court 2024

orgs.d: US investment bank. Its bankers arranged 1MDB's bond issues, from which money was diverted; it settled with Malaysia for about $3.9 billion in 2020. Its staff and former staff have often moved into top finance posts, and former European Commission President José Manuel Barroso chaired its international arm from 2016.
orgs.cite: Goldman–Malaysia settlement July 2020; EU ethics committee Oct 2016

orgs.d: Swiss-based commodity trader and miner, founded as Marc Rich + Co. In 2022 it pleaded guilty in the US and UK to bribing officials in several African and Latin American countries, and agreed to pay the DR Congo $180 million.
orgs.reach_src: UK SFO statement of facts; DRC settlement

orgs.d: Geneva-based oil trader. Swiss authorities penalised it in 2019 for failing to prevent bribery in Côte d'Ivoire and the Republic of Congo, and in 2024 it paid about $661 million to US and Swiss authorities over corruption in Ecuador.

Commodity trader founded in 1993. It pleaded guilty in the US in 2024 to bribing Petrobras officials in Brazil and was convicted in Switzerland in 2025 over bribes to an Angolan official (under appeal).
orgs.cite: US DOJ 2024; Swiss Federal Criminal Court 2025

orgs.d: Canadian engineering company, renamed AtkinsRéalis in 2023. It lobbied Ottawa for a deferred-prosecution law while facing bribery charges over Libya; Canada's Ethics Commissioner found in 2019 that Prime Minister Trudeau improperly pressed the Attorney General on its behalf.
orgs.cite: Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner, Aug 2019

orgs.d: Indian conglomerate in ports, airports, power and mining, founded by Gautam Adani. US prosecutors charged Adani and associates in November 2024 with a scheme of over $250 million in bribes to Indian officials; Kenya cancelled Adani deals the next day.
Ohio electric utility. It funnelled about $60 million to a group around Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder in return for a nuclear-plant bailout law (HB 6), and paid a $230 million penalty in 2021.

Chicago's electric utility, owned by Exelon. It admitted in a 2020 deferred prosecution agreement to a scheme of jobs and contracts for associates of Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan, who was convicted in 2025.
orgs.cite: US Attorney N.D. Ill.; verdict Feb 2025

orgs.d: Philippine company founded in 2019 with ₱625,000 in capital that won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic supply contracts; a Senate inquiry linked it to Michael Yang, a former adviser to President Duterte.

British political-data and campaign firm, part of SCL Group, that closed in 2018 after it was found to have harvested Facebook users' data. Its executives were recorded saying it ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns in Kenya.

Swedish tobacco company (snus), bought by Philip Morris International in 2022. An approach to it seeking €60 million for help with EU tobacco rules led to the departure of EU Health Commissioner John Dalli in 2012.

orgs.n: Sun Kian Ip Group (Ng Lap Seng)
orgs.d: Macau property group of Ng Lap Seng, who was convicted in New York in 2017 of bribing UN General Assembly President John Ashe to support a Macau conference centre.

orgs.n: Erik Prince security companies (Blackwater, Frontier Services Group, Vectus Global)
orgs.d: Erik Prince founded the private military company Blackwater in 1997 (sold 2010), chaired the Hong Kong-listed Frontier Services Group backed by China's state CITIC Group until 2021, and now runs Vectus Global. A UN panel found in 2021 he broke the Libya arms embargo; in 2025–26 his men worked with the governments of Ecuador, Haiti and the DR Congo.
orgs.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya 2021; Reuters 2025–26

orgs.d: Private US charity founded in 2000. In 2020 it was the WHO's second-largest contributor and it is a major funder of the vaccine alliance Gavi, which gives it influence over global health priorities.

Intergovernmental lender of last resort for 190 countries, created at Bretton Woods in 1944. Its loans come with policy conditions, and its staff move between the Fund and national finance ministries and central banks.

Intergovernmental development lender created in 1944. Its staff and managers often move into national cabinets (e.g. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Nigeria). A 2021 WilmerHale inquiry found its leadership altered Doing Business data for China; the bank stopped the report.

orgs.n: International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG)
