orgs.d: Commission created by a UN–Guatemala agreement of 12 December 2006 to help Guatemalan prosecutors dismantle criminal networks inside the state. It helped break up over 70 networks, brought the case that forced President Otto Pérez Molina to resign in 2015, and was shut down by President Jimmy Morales in 2019.

orgs.n: Tony Blair Institute for Global Change
orgs.d: Non-profit founded in 2016 by former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, absorbing his Africa Governance Initiative. It places advisers inside presidents' and prime ministers' offices; it reports work with governments in more than 45 countries and about 1,000 staff (2026). Its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia summary of TBI's published work

orgs.n: Russian state energy companies (Rosneft, Gazprom, Nord Stream)
orgs.d: Russia's state-controlled oil and gas companies and the Nord Stream pipeline company. They gave board seats to former European leaders, including German ex-chancellor Gerhard Schröder (Nord Stream from 2006, Rosneft from 2017) and Austrian ex-foreign minister Karin Kneissl (Rosneft 2021–22).

A generic key for Pentecostal, charismatic and evangelical Protestant churches when no single named church is the vehicle. Modern Pentecostalism is usually dated to the 1906 Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles. In Brazil these churches organise as the Evangelical Parliamentary Front (213 deputies and 26 senators registered in the current legislature); in Africa they supply heads of government and ministers, as in Ethiopia and Zambia. Each case record names the specific church.

orgs.n: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD)
orgs.d: A neo-Pentecostal church founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo, run on a tightly centralised model and active in many countries. Its pastors founded the Republicanos party in 2005, whose president Marcos Pereira is a UCKG bishop. Its bishops have held federal ministries and the mayoralty of Rio. It has faced bans or state takeovers abroad: Zambia banned it in 1998 and 2005 (both lifted on appeal) and Angola removed its Brazilian leadership in 2020.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God' and 'Republicanos'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia article (bans, investigations and press reports by country; Crivella's mission in South Africa)

orgs.hq: Redemption City of God, Mowe, Ogun State
orgs.d: A Nigerian holiness Pentecostal church founded in 1952 by Josiah Akindayomi, which reports a presence in 197 countries and territories and over 5 million members in Nigeria. Its pastors include Yemi Osinbajo, Vice President of Nigeria from 2015 to 2023, who is a senior pastor of its Lagos Province 48.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Redeemed Christian Church of God' and 'Yemi Osinbajo'

orgs.d: A US Christian lobbying group founded in 1999 by Sharon Slater after the World Congress of Families in Geneva, and still affiliated with it. It holds UN consultative status and campaigns in Africa against abortion, comprehensive sex education and homosexuality. A Ugandan activist named Slater as having lobbied for Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act; its African director ran a 2020 'Stop CSE' video campaign in Ethiopia.

A Sufi order founded in 1883 by Amadou Bamba, centred on the holy city of Touba, which has run with wide autonomy from the state since a 1928 French colonial deed. Its hereditary caliphs have long traded religious endorsement for state support: Senghor promised to fund Touba's Great Mosque, Diouf received a voting instruction (ndigal) from the caliph in 1988, and Abdoulaye Wade, a Mouride, went to Touba the day after his 2000 election. Presidents still visit the caliph before the annual Grand Magal pilgrimage.

Morocco's largest Sufi order, a branch of the Qadiriyya founded in north-eastern Morocco in the 1940s, with several hundred thousand followers and many adherents in France. The Moroccan state promotes Sufism as an alternative to Salafism, and Ahmed Toufiq, Minister of Islamic Affairs since 2002, has said a meeting with one of the order's sheikhs set him on the Sufi path.

orgs.n: Hereditary Sufi shrine lineages (pirs / makhdooms) of Pakistan
orgs.d: A generic key for families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines in Pakistan and draw income and votes from devotees. Several such families have sent members into national cabinets; Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of the Bahauddin Zakariya shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice.

Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, founded in 1926 by traditionalist scholars and merchants and organised around pesantren boarding schools; with over 40 million members in 2023 it is counted as the world's largest Islamic organisation. It was a political party in the 1950s–70s. Its supreme leader from 2015, Ma'ruf Amin, became Vice President of Indonesia in 2019.

The largest Orthodox church, led since 2009 by Patriarch Kirill, who backs Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its affiliated churches in neighbouring states have become targets of state action: Ukraine banned it by law in 2024, Estonia expelled the Moscow Patriarchate's metropolitan in 2024, and Latvia legislated its Orthodox church's independence in 2022. The UK, Canada and Ukraine sanctioned Kirill in 2022.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Patriarch Kirill of Moscow' and articles on the Ukrainian, Estonian and Latvian churches

orgs.d: A Saudi-funded international Islamic organisation founded in Mecca in 1962 to spread Islam abroad. A 1983 Belgian decree put the Great Mosque of Brussels under its control; Belgium ended the Saudi concession in 2018 on the recommendation of the parliamentary inquiry into the 2016 Brussels bombings. Its money also paid the first imams of Germany's DITIB.

orgs.n: Gulf state and private Salafi missionary funding networks
orgs.d: A key for Salafi mosque and preacher funding that a government body has documented as coming from Gulf states or donors there, when no single named organisation is identified. The Dutch parliamentary inquiry of 2020 named donors from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar and listed amounts given to individual Dutch mosques.
orgs.cite: Dutch parliamentary inquiry, 25 Jun 2020, via DutchNews

orgs.n: Diyanet (Presidency of Religious Affairs, Turkey) and its foreign branches (DITIB, ATIB)
orgs.d: Turkey's state religious directorate, founded in 1924. It writes the weekly sermon for about 85,000 mosques in Turkey and more than 2,000 abroad, employs imams as civil servants, and had a 2019 budget estimated at €1.7 billion. Its foreign arms include DITIB in Germany and ATIB in Austria. In 2016 it gave Turkey's parliament 50 reports from 38 countries on suspected Gülen followers gathered through its imams.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Presidency of Religious Affairs'; Hürriyet Daily News 2016
orgs.reach_src: Case records (government actions or findings in each country)

orgs.d: A Catholic men's fraternal and insurance order founded in New Haven in 1882, with councils in the United States, the Philippines and other countries. Members have included John F. Kennedy and Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Its policy positions became an issue in the 2018–19 Senate confirmation of judge Brian Buescher.

orgs.hq: Network without headquarters (founder C. Peter Wagner)
orgs.d: A loose network of charismatic Christian 'apostles' and 'prophets' shaped by C. Peter Wagner, whose 2008 book 'Dominion!' urged gaining political influence. Its 'Seven Mountains' teaching names government as one of seven spheres for Christians to take. Scholars say its standing grew after Trump's 2016 election; Wikipedia's account lists Speaker Mike Johnson, Pennsylvania senator Doug Mastriano and White House Faith Office head Paula White among associated figures.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'New Apostolic Reformation', citing André Gagné (2024) and others

orgs.d: A Philippine Pentecostal church begun in 1978 by Eddie Villanueva with a Bible-study group at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines. Villanueva also founded the Philippines for Jesus Movement of more than forty bishops; he ran for president in 2004 and 2010 and was a Deputy Speaker of the House from 2019 to 2022; his son Joel Villanueva is a senator.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Eddie Villanueva' and 'Jesus Is Lord Church'

orgs.d: A non-trinitarian church founded in Guadalajara in 1926 by Aarón Joaquín and led by his descendants. Its third leader, Naasón Joaquín García, was honoured at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in May 2019 at a senator's request, arrested in Los Angeles weeks later, and in June 2022 pleaded guilty to child sexual abuse and was sentenced to 16 years and 8 months. He continues to lead the church from prison.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'La Luz del Mundo' and 'Naasón Joaquín García'

orgs.n: Operation Rubicon / Thesaurus (CIA–BND ownership of Crypto AG)
orgs.d: Joint operation in which the US CIA and West German BND secretly owned the Swiss cipher-machine maker Crypto AG from 1970 (BND until about 1993, CIA until about 2018) and read the encrypted traffic of its government customers in more than 120 countries. Revealed by The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF on 11 February 2020.
orgs.cite: Washington Post/ZDF/SRF, 11 Feb 2020; Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020

orgs.d: The Saudi government and officials around Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Recorded here for paying a Twitter employee to pass on data about critics (US conviction 2022) and for the 2017–19 Ritz-Carlton detentions in which business owners handed assets to the state.
orgs.cite: US v. Abouammo (N.D. Cal. 2022); Saudi anti-corruption committee statement 2019

orgs.d: North Korea sends programmers, mostly working from China and Russia, to take remote jobs at foreign companies under stolen or fake identities, helped by 'laptop farms' run by paid facilitators; wages fund the state's weapons programmes. US prosecutors have found workers at hundreds of US firms, and Google reported a move into Europe in 2025.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice cases 2024–26; Google Threat Intelligence Group, Apr 2025

orgs.n: Lazarus Group / TraderTraitor (North Korean state hackers)
orgs.d: Hacking units of North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau that steal cryptocurrency and break into companies, often through suppliers and fake job offers. The FBI attributed the US$1.5 billion Bybit theft of February 2025 to them.

China's civilian intelligence and security ministry. It runs officers who recruit employees of foreign firms (Xu Yanjun, convicted in the US 2021) and is widely credited with the Salt Typhoon intrusions into telecom companies in some 80 countries.
orgs.cite: US v. Xu Yanjun (S.D. Ohio 2021); 13-country joint advisory Aug 2025

orgs.d: Russia's foreign intelligence service. The US government attributed the 2019–20 SolarWinds Orion supply-chain intrusion to it in 2021.

The US signals-intelligence agency. It designed the Dual_EC random-number generator whose weakness was used in the backdoor found in Juniper's ScreenOS in 2015. (Not to be confused with the existing key us_nsa, the National Student Association.)
orgs.cite: Juniper advisory Dec 2015; Checkoway et al.

orgs.n: Russian intelligence services (FSB, GRU) acting through companies and insiders
orgs.d: Russia's security (FSB) and military intelligence (GRU) services as they reach into companies: recruiting employees (SoftBank 2020; ASML/NXP 2025), suspected access through software makers (Kaspersky), and pressure in corporate disputes (Baring Vostok 2019).
orgs.cite: Court records in Japan and the Netherlands; US Commerce Department 2024

orgs.d: Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of Wirecard until June 2020, is described by German investigators and the UK Crown Prosecution Service as working for Russian intelligence. From Russia he directed a Bulgarian spy cell in Britain (convicted 2025) and received material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott (convicted 2026).

orgs.n: Chinese state talent-recruitment plans (Thousand Talents and local equivalents)
orgs.d: Government programmes that recruit scientists and engineers working abroad. US prosecutors have tied members to theft of company secrets, e.g. GE's Xiaoqing Zheng (Thousand Talents) and Google's Linwei Ding (applied to a Shanghai plan).
orgs.cite: US v. Zheng (N.D.N.Y. 2022); US v. Ding (N.D. Cal. 2026)

orgs.d: Russia's state corporation for defence and industrial technology. Ukrainian prosecutors charge that Motor Sich's former management colluded with it to supply engines for Russian helicopters.

Israel's foreign intelligence agency. According to the New York Times it ran BAC Consulting in Budapest and other shell firms that supplied booby-trapped pagers to Hezbollah under a Taiwanese brand licence; Israel's prime minister acknowledged the operation in November 2024.
orgs.cite: PM Netanyahu statement 10 Nov 2024; New York Times

orgs.n: Chinese Communist Party organisations inside companies
orgs.d: Under the PRC Company Law any firm with three or more party members must set up a party organisation. 73.1% of private firms had one in 2018; all top state firms wrote the party's role into their charters in 2017, and some foreign joint ventures were asked to do the same.
orgs.cite: PRC Company Law; CCP Organization Department; CSIS

orgs.d: Presidential decree of April 2023 letting the Russian state take over management of assets owned by companies from 'unfriendly' countries; used against Fortum, Uniper, Danone and Carlsberg in 2023.

orgs.n: IRGC business empire (Khatam al-Anbiya and IRGC foundations)
orgs.d: The Revolutionary Guards' economic arm. Khatam al-Anbiya controls more than 812 companies and is designated by the UN (2010), US (2007) and EU (2008); IRGC-linked foundations bought control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran in 2009.
Turkish state fund that became trustee of companies seized by the government; it took over 784 companies accused of Gülen links after 2015–16 and controlled 1,056 businesses in all by October 2025.
orgs.cite: Turkish Treasury figures via Anadolu Agency

orgs.d: Shanghai-listed electronics company, almost 30% traceable to Chinese state shareholders, which bought the Dutch chipmaker Nexperia in 2018; the Dutch state took control of Nexperia's governance in October 2025.
orgs.cite: Dutch Goods Availability Act order Oct 2025

orgs.d: Chinese state-owned chemicals group, largest shareholder of Pirelli; Italy limited its control by a golden-power decree in 2023.
Private Shandong energy and logistics company owned by Ye Cheng, who has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party; holds a 99-year lease of Port Darwin (2015) that Australia now seeks to reverse.
China's state-owned power-grid company, the world's largest utility; owns 40% of the Philippines' national grid operator and holds grid stakes in several other countries.
Chinese wind-turbine maker convicted by a US jury in 2018 of stealing AMSC's control software through an insider at AMSC's Austrian unit.
orgs.cite: US District Court W.D. Wisconsin, 24 Jan 2018

orgs.d: Chinese state-backed memory-chip maker charged in the US (2018) with Micron trade-secret theft through UMC engineers; put on the US export blacklist in 2018 and acquitted at trial in February 2024.
orgs.cite: US District Court N.D. California, 27 Feb 2024

orgs.d: Japanese chip-equipment maker whose Taiwan unit was fined in April 2026 after staff obtained TSMC's 2nm secrets to win orders.

orgs.n: CHJS (Chengdu chip venture of Choi Jin-seok)
orgs.d: Chip venture set up by former Samsung executive Choi Jin-seok with about US$340 million from the Chengdu government; Korean prosecutors say it was built on Samsung plant plans and process data.
Brazil's largest criminal organisation, born in São Paulo's prisons, now trading cocaine internationally and laundering money through fuel, fintech and transport companies.
orgs.cite: São Paulo Public Ministry, Operação Fim da Linha 2024

orgs.d: The Sicilian Mafia, made of family clans such as the Laudani of Catania, which in 2017 placed firms inside Lidl Italia's supply contracts in Lombardy.
Calabrian mafia organised by families, with branches across northern Italy and abroad; courts have found it owning and steering construction and haulage firms in Emilia-Romagna (Aemilia trial).
orgs.cite: Court of Cassation, Aemilia rulings 2018 and 2022

orgs.d: Japan's organised-crime syndicates, such as the Yamaguchi-gumi, historically active through construction and property companies; 9,400 members and 8,200 associates in 2025 per the National Police Agency.
Groups calling themselves business forums that force their way onto building sites and demand 30% of contract value; spread from KwaZulu-Natal to Gauteng and the Cape.

orgs.n: Ransomware and data-extortion groups that recruit insiders
orgs.d: Criminal groups that bribe or recruit company employees and contractors to plant malware or copy customer data, then demand ransom (Tesla 2020, Coinbase 2025).
orgs.cite: US v. Kriuchkov (D. Nev. 2021); Coinbase disclosure 2025

orgs.d: Jihadist armed movement that held territory in Syria and Iraq in 2014–19 and took payments from companies operating there, including Lafarge (convicted in Paris, April 2026).
orgs.cite: Paris Criminal Court 13 Apr 2026; US plea Oct 2022

orgs.d: US maker of airliners and military aircraft. Under the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization its own employees carry out much of the safety certification of its planes. Congressional and Inspector General inquiries after the 737 MAX crashes of 2018–2019 found it withheld information from the regulator.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Sackler-owned maker of OxyContin. Pleaded guilty to misbranding in 2007 and to federal charges again in 2020; went through bankruptcy and is being restructured.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: US drug distribution industry (McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen/Cencora)
orgs.d: The three largest US wholesale drug distributors and their trade association. Reporting in 2017 tied a 2016 law that weakened DEA enforcement to industry lobbying and former DEA staff.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Monsanto, maker of the herbicide Roundup (glyphosate) and genetically modified seeds, was bought by Bayer in 2018. Cases show a bribe to an Indonesian official (2002), contacts with an EPA manager, and industry text in Germany's glyphosate review.
orgs.cite: US DOJ/SEC 2005; MDL 2741 documents; Weber & Burtscher-Schaden 2019
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Florida's largest electric utility. Leaked records of its consultant Matrix LLC tied FPL-linked money to the 2020 'ghost candidate' Senate races; FPL was not charged and denies wrongdoing.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Largest US oil company. In 2021 its federal lobbyist was filmed describing weekly contact with a key senator's office and use of 'shadow groups'.
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Elon Musk's companies (Tesla, SpaceX, Neuralink, xAI)
orgs.d: Companies controlled by Elon Musk, who led the Department of Government Efficiency in 2025 while they faced federal enforcement actions. A Senate minority staff memo estimated $2.37 billion in liabilities at stake.
orgs.cite: US Senate PSI minority staff memorandum, 27 April 2025

Icelandic fishing company. The 2019 Fishrot Files showed payments to people close to Namibia's government for fishing quotas; two Namibian ministers were charged under organised-crime law and Iceland opened an investigation.

Cigarette and narcotics smuggling network that a Podgorica court found was led by Miloš Medenica and shielded by his mother, former Supreme Court president Vesna Medenica; both were sentenced in January 2026.

Business and political network of Vlad Plahotniuc, leader of the Democratic Party of Moldova, who was described as controlling the government and parliamentary majority until 2019. He was convicted in April 2026 over the 2014 theft of about $1 billion from Moldovan banks.
Scheme that moved $20–80 billion out of Russia in 2010–14 by having Moldovan judges enforce fake debts, then routing the money through Moldindconbank and Latvian banks to companies worldwide.

Gang led by Sergei Tsapok in Krasnodar Krai that murdered 12 people in November 2010 after years operating under the protection of local authorities. Tsapok was convicted and died in prison in 2014.

Banned Kenyan sect and gang that ran extortion in Nairobi's minibus transport and slums. The Waki Commission linked it to organised revenge attacks in the 2007–08 post-election violence; ICC charges against Uhuru Kenyatta over it were withdrawn in 2014.

orgs.n: Rothschild family banks (N M Rothschild & Sons; Rothschild & Co)
orgs.hq: New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London; Paris
orgs.d: Banking family descended from Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt, whose five sons set up houses in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples. The London house (1811) managed British war subsidies in the Napoleonic Wars, lent to Prussia, Brazil and others, financed the 1835 slave-compensation loan and the 1875 Suez Canal share purchase; the family dominated European finance from the 1820s to the 1870s. Today's Rothschild & Co (Paris-listed, controlled by the French and English branches) is mainly an advisory bank for mergers, debt restructuring and governments. The family has been the main target of antisemitic conspiracy theories since the 1840s; such claims are recorded separately as contested.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Rothschild family', 'Rothschild & Co'; N. Ferguson, The House of Rothschild (1998)

orgs.hq: 23 Wall Street (historic); 270 Park Avenue, New York
orgs.d: Founded as Drexel, Morgan & Co. in 1871 and renamed J.P. Morgan & Co. in 1895, with London (Morgan, Grenfell) and Paris (Morgan, Harjes) affiliates. It rescued the US Treasury's gold in 1895, organised the 1907 panic rescue, was Britain's and France's financial agent in the US in 1914–17, and its partners held top public posts (Lamont, Morrow, Leffingwell, Gilbert). The 1913 Pujo Committee found Morgan-linked men held 341 directorships in 112 corporations. It merged into Chase Manhattan in 2000 to form JPMorgan Chase, which in 2016 paid $264 million over hiring relatives of Chinese officials.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan', 'JPMorgan Chase', 'Pujo Committee'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope pp. 52–53

orgs.d: New York investment bank led from 1885 by Jacob Schiff, with partners Paul and Felix Warburg; it financed US railroads and, in 1904–05, about $200 million of Japanese war bonds. Paul Warburg drafted much of the 1910 Jekyll Island plan and sat on the first Federal Reserve Board. Antisemitic writers later falsely claimed the firm financed the Bolsheviks. It merged with Lehman Brothers in 1977.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Jacob Schiff', 'Paul Warburg'; P. Roberts, American Jewish Archives Journal 49 (1997)

orgs.d: Hamburg private bank founded in 1798 by Moses Marcus and Gerson Warburg; still about 40% Warburg-owned. Max Warburg, its head 1910–38, advised Kaiser Wilhelm II, served at Versailles as an expert and sat on the Reichsbank council; the Nazis 'Aryanised' the bank in 1938. In the 2010s it was implicated in cum-ex tax fraud; a €47 million tax claim was dropped in 2016 after its co-owner met Hamburg mayor Olaf Scholz, the subject of a parliamentary inquiry. The tax was repaid in 2020.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'M. M. Warburg & Co.'; German Wikipedia 'Max Warburg'

orgs.d: Investment bank founded in New Orleans in 1848 that grew into allied houses in New York, Paris and London; it advised the French government on gold buying from the 1850s. Lazard Brothers in London was led by Robert Kindersley and Robert Brand, whom Carroll Quigley places at the centre of the Milner/Round Table group. Felix Rohatyn of Lazard ran New York City's 1975 rescue; its Sovereign Advisory group has advised Greece, Argentina, Lebanon and others on debt, and it advised the UK on the 2013 Royal Mail sale.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Lazard'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment; NAO (2014)

orgs.d: London merchant bank founded in 1762 by Francis Baring. With Hope & Co. it financed the Louisiana Purchase (1803) and was called 'the sixth great European power' in 1818. It was rescued by a Bank of England-led consortium in 1890 after Argentine losses, and collapsed in 1995 after Nick Leeson's £827 million trading losses in Singapore; ING bought it for £1. Family member Evelyn Baring (Lord Cromer) ran Egypt's finances as British controller and consul-general (1879–1907).
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Barings Bank', 'Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer'

orgs.n: Wallenberg family sphere (Stockholms Enskilda Bank, SEB, Investor AB)
orgs.d: Swedish banking and industrial family; André Oscar Wallenberg founded Stockholms Enskilda Bank in 1856 (merged into SEB in 1972). Through Investor AB, where family foundations hold just over 50% of votes, it controls or holds major stakes in Ericsson, ABB, Saab, Atlas Copco, SEB and others. In the Second World War its bankers led Swedish trade talks with Germany and the Allies, and the US seized American Bosch and blacklisted the bank (1945–47) over cloaking of German assets.

Formed by the 1955 merger of the Rockefeller-linked Chase National Bank and the Bank of the Manhattan Company; David Rockefeller was its president from 1960 and chairman and chief executive from 1969 to 1980/81, also chairing the Council on Foreign Relations (1970–85) and founding the Trilateral Commission (1973). Chase opened the first US bank branch in Moscow (1973) and in 1979 led the campaign to admit the Shah of Iran to the US. It merged with J.P. Morgan & Co. in 2000.

Founded in 1930 under the Young Plan to handle German reparations, owned by member central banks, and the oldest international financial institution. It hosts closed meetings of central bank governors (monthly in the 1930s, every two months since 1998) and the Basel Committee whose capital rules countries adopt. In 1939 it transferred Czechoslovakia's gold to the Reichsbank; the 1944 Bretton Woods conference called for its liquidation, reversed in 1948. Carroll Quigley called it 'the apex' of a private world system of financial control.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope pp. 324–325

orgs.d: Swiss bank founded in 1856 and taken over by UBS in 2023. Its bankers arranged Mozambique's hidden 'tuna bond' loans of 2013–14 and took kickbacks; the bank pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US in 2021, was fined almost $500 million and forgave $200 million of Mozambique's debt. In 2014 and 2025 it pleaded guilty in US tax-evasion cases.

The world's largest asset manager. It was retained by the US Treasury in 2009, managed the Federal Reserve's corporate bond-buying programmes in 2020, and was given a role in planning Ukraine's reconstruction in 2022. Former staff include Brian Deese (Biden's National Economic Council director) and Friedrich Merz (chairman of BlackRock Germany 2016–20, Chancellor from 2025).

Formed by the 1998 Travelers–Citicorp merger, made legal by the 1999 repeal of Glass–Steagall; former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin joined as chairman of its executive committee in 1999. Citigroup executive Michael Froman sent Barack Obama's transition a cabinet list in October 2008 that largely matched the eventual appointments. Citigroup received a federal rescue in 2008.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Rubin', 'Michael Froman'; The New Republic, 14 Oct 2016

orgs.d: Brazilian bank owned by the Rabello family whose branches supplied cash for the 2005 'mensalão' payments to deputies; its president Kátia Rabello was convicted by the Supreme Federal Court in 2012. The Central Bank of Brazil put it into liquidation in 2013.
orgs.cite: Supreme Federal Court AP 470; Portuguese Wikipedia 'Kátia Rabello'

orgs.n: Banco Espírito Santo / Grupo Espírito Santo
orgs.d: Portuguese bank of the Espírito Santo family, led by Ricardo Salgado ('Dono Disto Tudo'); it collapsed in August 2014 and its good assets became Novo Banco. In Operation Marquês prosecutors link Espírito Santo group payments to former Prime Minister José Sócrates; the trial began in July 2025.

Not one body but the core of Lebanon's banking sector: a 2016 study found 18 of the 20 largest banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, holding about 43% of sector assets. The banks financed the state and the Banque du Liban under Riad Salameh until the 2019 collapse froze deposits.

St Petersburg bank whose largest shareholder is Yury Kovalchuk; the US Treasury called it 'the personal bank for senior officials of the Russian Federation' when sanctioning it in March 2014. It expanded into annexed Crimea and is under US, EU and other sanctions.

Ukraine's largest bank, co-founded by Ihor Kolomoisky and Gennadiy Bogolyubov; nationalised in December 2016 with a $5.6 billion bailout after insider lending. Kolomoisky was designated by the US for significant corruption in 2021 and arrested in Ukraine in 2023. The bank is now state-owned.

Philanthropy founded in 1913 from the Standard Oil fortune of John D. Rockefeller; by the 1920s the world's largest. Its International Health Division ran campaigns with governments, it funded League of Nations bodies and the Institute of Pacific Relations, and its 1943 Mexican Agriculture Program began the Green Revolution later spread to India and elsewhere.

The NSA is the US signals-intelligence agency. Documents leaked by Edward Snowden in 2013 showed it monitoring allied leaders, EU institutions and UN headquarters, often with partner services such as Denmark's FE and Germany's BND.
GCHQ is the UK's signals-intelligence agency. Snowden documents showed it intercepting delegates at the 2009 London G20 and hacking Belgium's state telecom Belgacom in 2010–2013.

The CIA is the US foreign intelligence and covert-action agency. With West Germany's BND it secretly owned the Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG from 1970 to 2018, and in 2025 President Trump confirmed authorising it to carry out covert action in Venezuela.
orgs.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020; Trump statement Oct 2025

orgs.d: Swiss maker of cipher machines sold to more than 120 governments. Secretly owned by the CIA and BND from 1970 (BND until about 1993, CIA until 2018), its machines were rigged so the two services could read customers' messages. Liquidated in 2018.
reach_est: more than 120 customer states, not all named

orgs.d: Australia's foreign intelligence service. In 2004 it bugged Timor-Leste's cabinet room during Timor Sea oil-and-gas talks; the resulting treaty was later replaced.

Tel Aviv political marketing firm that, per the New York Times, ran a roughly $2m covert social-media campaign aimed at US lawmakers for Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs in 2023–24. Meta banned it in May 2024.
orgs.cite: New York Times, June 2024; Meta threat report May 2024

orgs.d: Geneva private intelligence firm founded by Mario Brero. Leaked files reported in 2023 ('Abu Dhabi Secrets') show the UAE paid it at least €5.7m from 2017 to target about 1,000 people and 400 organisations in 18 European countries.

Emirati cyber firm that from 2016 ran Project Raven, a UAE surveillance unit staffed partly by former US intelligence operatives, which Reuters reported targeted Qatar's emir, activists and journalists. Three ex-US operatives signed US deferred-prosecution agreements in 2021.
India's foreign intelligence agency. Two RAW officers were reported expelled from Australia in 2020 after ASIO disrupted a 'nest of spies'; an officer was also charged in the US Pannun murder plot.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: Pakistan's main military intelligence agency. It funded the Kashmiri American Council's lobbying in Washington (Fai plea, 2011), and the US military's top officer called the Haqqani network its 'veritable arm' in 2011.
Egypt's main intelligence service. German prosecutors charged an employee of the German federal government's press office in 2020 with working for it since 2010.

Cuba's foreign intelligence service. It recruited US DIA analyst Ana Montes (convicted 2002) and ex-ambassador Víctor Manuel Rocha, and under 2008 agreements Cuba's defence ministry advised the restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence.
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: North Korea's main foreign intelligence and cyber body. US agencies tie it to the 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist and to schemes placing North Korean IT workers inside foreign companies.

orgs.n: GRU (Main Directorate of the General Staff), Russia
orgs.d: Russia's military intelligence service. Its officers were caught trying to hack the OPCW in The Hague in 2018 and were indicted in the US for hacking WADA after the McLaren report.
orgs.cite: Dutch MoD Oct 2018; US indictment Oct 2018

orgs.d: Russia's domestic security service. The McLaren reports (2016) found it helped swap athletes' urine samples at the 2014 Sochi Olympics as part of a state-directed doping cover-up.
South Korea's intelligence agency (formerly KCIA). US prosecutors in 2024 charged CFR scholar Sue Mi Terry with acting as its unregistered agent since 2013; the case was deferred in 2026.
Indian company group that EU DisinfoLab linked in 2019–2020 to hundreds of fake news sites and revived NGOs used to lobby the UN Human Rights Council and European Parliament against Pakistan.
Project begun in 2014 by Iran's Foreign Ministry to cultivate Iranian-heritage academics in Western think tanks, revealed by leaked emails in 2023 (Semafor, Iran International).

orgs.n: Office of the High Representative (OHR), Bosnia and Herzegovina
orgs.d: International office created by the 1995 Dayton agreement and overseen by the Peace Implementation Council of foreign governments. Its 1997 'Bonn powers' let it impose laws and dismiss Bosnian officials (139 removed by 2004).
Regional central bank issuing the Central African CFA franc for six states. Under its arrangement with France, the French Treasury guarantees the peg and members deposit half their reserves with it.

Foundation jointly run by the Olympic movement and governments that sets anti-doping rules worldwide. Its McLaren reports found Russian state doping; GRU hackers later attacked it; the US has criticised its handling of Chinese swimmers' 2021 positive tests.
Governing body of track and field. Its president 1999–2015, Lamine Diack, was convicted in Paris in 2020 of taking money to cover up Russian doping.

The UN Secretariat in New York and offices such as the human rights office (OHCHR) in Geneva. Cases include NSA bugging of the headquarters, Saudi pressure on the Secretary-General's child-rights list (2016) and OHCHR sharing activists' names with China.

orgs.n: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW)
orgs.d: Treaty body that enforces the Chemical Weapons Convention. In April 2018 four GRU officers were caught trying to hack its Wi-Fi network while it investigated the Salisbury Novichok poisoning.

Permanent court trying individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. A 2024 press investigation reported Israeli intelligence spied on and pressured its prosecutors for nearly a decade.

Governments that sell citizenship or passports, and the agents and buyers around them. Cases include sanctioned Iranians in St Kitts (FinCEN 2014), the Cyprus Papers (2020), Comoros's sale of passports to Gulf bidoon (Sambi convicted 2022) and diplomatic posts linked to donors in Dominica and Grenada (Al Jazeera 2019).
orgs.cite: FinCEN FIN-2014-A004; Al Jazeera Investigative Unit; OCCRP

orgs.d: Five companies linked to UK businessman Zuneth Sattar that won 16 Malawi police and army contracts worth over 150 million dollars in 2017–2021, according to Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau (2022).

Groups moving South American cocaine to Europe and the US, including the FARC in the 2000s–2010s, that have bought or recruited military and security chiefs along their routes (Guinea-Bissau, Suriname).

orgs.n: Benjamin Bol Mel and his companies
orgs.d: South Sudanese businessman close to President Kiir, sanctioned by the US for corruption in 2017; vice president Feb–Nov 2025.
Danish power-plant builder debarred by the African Development Bank in 2020 for paying Mauritian officials through intermediaries in the Saint-Louis power station tender.
Jihadist network founded by Osama bin Laden. UN monitors report it keeps close ties with Afghanistan's Taliban government and that some Taliban leaders are affiliated with it.
Russian property and energy group of Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan; ran Electric Networks of Armenia until Armenia moved to nationalise it after his 2025 arrest.

orgs.n: Zhao Wei Transnational Criminal Organization (Kings Romans)
orgs.d: Casino group of Zhao Wei that leases and runs Laos's Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone; designated by the US Treasury in 2018 for drug trafficking and money laundering.

Chinese Communist Party department that handles relations with foreign political parties. In Dec 2020 its vice-minister Guo Yezhou led a delegation to Nepal during the split in the ruling Nepal Communist Party.

orgs.n: VimpelCom, Telia and MTS (Uzbek telecom bribery)
orgs.d: Three telecom groups that admitted in US settlements (2016, 2017, 2019) to paying entities controlled by Gulnara Karimova for access to Uzbekistan's mobile market.

orgs.n: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou (Rongelap SAR scheme)
orgs.d: China-born businesspeople who bribed Marshall Islands legislators in 2016–2020 to create a semi-autonomous Rongelap zone; both pleaded guilty in New York and were sentenced in 2023.
Phosphate trader charged by Australian prosecutors with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians in 2007–2012.

Firms paid by Australia's Home Affairs department to run asylum centres on Nauru and Manus Island. A 2023 SMH/Age investigation reported millions in subcontracts and payments reaching Nauruan and PNG political figures.

orgs.n: Wan Kuok-koi and World Hongmen History and Culture Association
orgs.d: Association led by former 14K triad boss Wan Kuok-koi, sanctioned by the US in 2020 as a criminal front; OCCRP documented its 2018–2019 attempt to set up a casino zone in Palau with former Palauan officials as directors.
Swiss bank. A Papua New Guinea Commission of Inquiry (2021) found the 2014 UBS-arranged loan to buy Oil Search shares unlawful and recommended a 10-year ban on UBS in PNG.
orgs.cite: PNG Commission of Inquiry into the UBS Loan

orgs.d: Albanian-Italian group dismantled by Italian police in 2017 for moving over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis; cousins of former interior minister Saimir Tahiri.
Andorran bank named a primary money-laundering concern by FinCEN in 2015 and taken over by the state; FinCEN withdrew the finding in 2016 and Spanish courts later cleared it.
Hungarian oil company. Croatian courts convicted ex-PM Ivo Sanader of taking a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive Zsolt Hernádi for control of INA; MOL denies it.
Helicopter company of Russian businessman Yuri Borisov, whose donations to President Paksas and the citizenship decree that followed led to Paksas's 2004 impeachment.

Dubai company of Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech, named in leaked papers as a planned payer to Panama companies of Malta's PM's chief of staff and energy minister; Fenech is charged over the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Russian billionaire and AS Monaco owner; a Monaco corruption probe (2018) over his dealings with officials was closed in 2025 because the evidence was unlawfully obtained.
Entrepreneurs and politicians in San Marino whose bribes for building permits and banking licences ran through an account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini'; convictions 2017, upheld 2022.

Finnish state-owned defence company; bribery allegations over its 2006 Slovenian armoured-vehicle deal led to a 2013 conviction of Janez Janša that was later annulled; two executives were convicted in Finland over Croatian deals.

orgs.n: Stanford Financial Group / Stanford International Bank
orgs.d: Allen Stanford's offshore bank, a 7 billion dollar fraud; Antigua's chief financial regulator was indicted in the US for taking its bribes.
Transnational gang. A 2023 US indictment says Salvadoran officials negotiated benefits for its jailed leaders in return for fewer killings and electoral support.
Guyanese gold trading firm of Nazar and Azruddin Mohamed, sanctioned by the US in 2024 for gold smuggling, tax evasion and bribing officials.

channels.n: Ambrosiano money: Milan → Nassau → Lima → Managua
channels.d: Banco Ambrosiano ran its offshore business through Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau and Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima, and funded both the Somoza regime and the Sandinista opposition in Nicaragua. The Vatican Bank was its main shareholder. When it collapsed in 1982, $1.287 billion could not be accounted for.

channels.n: IOR settlement: Vatican City → Ambrosiano creditors in Milan
channels.d: Archbishop Marcinkus's IOR allegedly issued letters of patronage backing Ambrosiano's foreign units. The IOR denied legal liability but acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to the creditors.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

channels.n: Calvi's flight: Milan → London (Blackfriars Bridge, 1982)
channels.d: Roberto Calvi, Ambrosiano chairman and P2 member, fled Italy on a false passport as the bank failed. He was found hanging from Blackfriars Bridge on 18 June 1982; Italian authorities reopened it as murder and prosecuted Licio Gelli and Giuseppe Calò.

channels.n: P2 lodge: Arezzo/Rome → Buenos Aires
channels.d: Gelli held an honorary diplomatic post at Argentina's Rome embassy and had ties to Perón and the junta. P2 members in Argentina included junta member Emilio Massera and Social Welfare Minister José López Rega, founder of the Triple A death squad; Raúl Lastiri was briefly interim president in 1973.

channels.n: P2 lodges in South America: Rome → Montevideo / São Paulo / Caracas
channels.d: P2 had lodges in Uruguay, Brazil and Venezuela as well as Argentina and Chile. Gelli took refuge in Uruguay in 1981 after his list was found.

channels.n: Gelli's escape: Arezzo → Geneva (1982–88)
channels.d: Gelli was arrested in Geneva in 1982 while trying to withdraw money, escaped prison in 1983, surrendered in 1987 and was extradited to Italy in 1988.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC/CPC → Rome (Gladio)
channels.d: NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee and the Allied Clandestine Committee coordinated national stay-behind plans. Andreotti said the last ACC meeting took place on 23–24 October 1990 under Belgian General Van Calster, the day before he disclosed Gladio and its 622 listed members to parliament.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Ankara (Counter-Guerrilla)
channels.d: Turkey's stay-behind branch was the Counter-Guerrilla, whose existence Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit revealed in 1973. Former prosecutor Emin Değer documented its ties to the Grey Wolves.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Athens (LOK / Sheepskin)
channels.d: Greece's network was the LOK mountain raider units, with a branch called Operation Sheepskin; the Greek defence minister said it operated until 1988.

channels.n: Stay-behind coordination: NATO ACC → Brussels / The Hague / Copenhagen
channels.d: Belgium's parliamentary committee found the ACC coordinated networks in ten countries. Dutch PM Ruud Lubbers informed parliament of a secret organisation in the defence ministry in 1990; arms caches were found near Rozendaal (1983) and Velp. Denmark's network was Absalon.

channels.n: Condor founding: Santiago → Buenos Aires → Montevideo → Asunción → La Paz
channels.d: Chile's DINA convened intelligence chiefs in Santiago on 25 November 1975; Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia signed the founding document in January 1976. Members shared intelligence and carried out cross-border kidnappings, torture and killings; Automotores Orletti in Buenos Aires was a key detention site.
channels.cite: US National Security Archive 2025 briefing book

channels.n: Condor expansion: Santiago → Brasília → Lima → Quito
channels.d: Brazil became a formal member in 1976; Peru and Ecuador joined in 1977–78. In 1980 Peruvian and Argentine agents kidnapped four Montonero militants in Lima, one of the last recorded Condor operations.
channels.cite: US National Security Archive 2025 briefing book

channels.n: Condor phase three: Santiago → Washington (Letelier, 1976)
channels.d: Former Chilean ambassador Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt were killed by a car bomb in Washington in September 1976; an FBI report suggested it may have been a Condor 'phase three' mission. The Letelier case led to the 1979 public revelation of Condor.
channels.cite: US National Security Archive 2025 briefing book

channels.n: Condor: La Paz exile killed in Buenos Aires (1976)
channels.d: Former Bolivian president Juan José Torres was assassinated in Buenos Aires in 1976, a case listed among Condor's cross-border killings.

channels.n: Safari Club: Riyadh money, Paris airlift, Rabat & Cairo troops → Shaba (Zaire, 1977)
channels.d: Saudi Arabia paid, France supplied technology and Egypt and Morocco provided troops. In 1977 French aircraft flew Moroccan and Egyptian troops into Zaire's Shaba province to repel an invasion.

channels.n: Safari Club arms: Cairo → Mogadishu (Ogaden war)
channels.d: The club supplied arms to Somalia in exchange for Siad Barre distancing himself from the Soviet Union during the Ogaden war. BCCI reportedly helped finance and launder money for the club's operations.

channels.n: Aginter Press: Lisbon → Milan / Rome (explosives training)
channels.d: Judge Guido Salvini found Aginter instructors trained members of the Italian neo-fascist Avanguardia Nazionale in explosives, and linked the agency to the groups behind the December 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing in Milan.

channels.n: Aginter Press: Lisbon → Luanda / Lourenço Marques (colonial wars)
channels.d: Aginter allegedly worked against independence movements in Portugal's colonies of Angola, Mozambique and East Timor; disputed sources tie it to the killings of Amílcar Cabral and Eduardo Mondlane.

channels.n: Aginter Press flight: Lisbon → Alicante / Caracas (1974)
channels.d: After the April 1974 Carnation Revolution, members fled to a site near Alicante associated with the Paladin Group, and the agency reportedly escaped to Caracas.

channels.n: WACL / Taiwan covert aid: Taipei → Tegucigalpa (Contras)
channels.d: After the 1987 Iran-Contra revelations, reports showed Taiwanese covert military aid to the Contras, who were based in Honduras; League chairman Ku Cheng-kang reportedly helped arrange it and Taiwan's Foreign Ministry confirmed the activity.

channels.n: CAUSA: New York → Contras in Honduras / Nicaragua
channels.d: CAUSA International, founded by the Unification movement in New York in 1980 and active in 21 Latin American countries, aided the Nicaraguan Contras.

channels.n: Unification Church: Seoul → Tokyo (dissolution case)
channels.d: Japan holds a large share of the church's membership. The Tokyo District Court ordered the Japanese religious corporation dissolved on 25 March 2025; the order was upheld in 2026.

channels.n: Snow White: Saint Hill → Los Angeles → Washington (IRS, Justice Dept)
channels.d: The Guardian's Office, headquartered at Saint Hill Manor in England with a US base in Los Angeles, ran infiltration of US federal agencies. The FBI caught two operatives in a federal courthouse in 1976 and raided church offices on 8 July 1977; eleven executives were convicted in 1979.
channels.cite: United States v. Hubbard; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'

channels.n: Snow White: Saint Hill → Toronto (infiltration of public offices)
channels.d: Operation Snow White extended to Canada. In 1992 the church was convicted in Ontario of breach of public trust for infiltrating public offices.
channels.cite: R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992)

channels.n: Gülen movement base: İzmir → Saylorsburg, Pennsylvania (1999)
channels.d: The movement began in İzmir, where Gülen set up student boarding houses from 1966; it moved its base to Pennsylvania in 1999, where Gülen lived until his death in October 2024.

channels.n: School seizures: Ankara → Bishkek (Sapat schools to Maarif)
channels.d: After 2016 Turkey pressed governments to close or hand over Gülen-linked schools. Kyrgyzstan transferred management of the Gülen-linked Sapat schools to Turkey; Turkey's Maarif Foundation said in 2021 it had taken over 216 schools in 44 countries.
channels.cite: Stockholm Center for Freedom; Turkish Minute (2021)

channels.n: Brotherhood branches → Hamas: Cairo / Amman → Gaza
channels.d: Hamas began in 1987 as a Brotherhood offshoot. On 13 January 2026 the US Treasury designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches as Specially Designated Global Terrorists for support to Hamas.
channels.cite: US Treasury designation 13 Jan 2026 (Times of Israel)

channels.n: Hizb ut-Tahrir coup attempts: Jerusalem → Amman / Damascus (1968–69)
channels.d: The party, founded in Jerusalem in 1953, was allegedly involved in two failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69, and in Egypt in 1974.

channels.n: Le Cercle: Paris → Bonn (founding axis)
channels.d: Antoine Pinay and Jean Violet founded the circle in 1952–53 with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss; Franco-German reconciliation was an early aim.

channels.n: Le Cercle: Paris / London → Pretoria (apartheid delegation)
channels.d: South Africa sent the only official government delegation to the circle; in the 1970s–80s it was tied to the apartheid state and backed Renamo and UNITA.

channels.n: Bilderberg → Val-Duchesse dinner: Oosterbeek → Brussels (2009)
channels.d: In November 2009, outside its annual conference, Bilderberg held a dinner at the Château of Val-Duchesse in Brussels to promote Herman Van Rompuy's candidacy for President of the European Council.

channels.n: Trilateral Commission → Carter administration: New York → Washington
channels.d: The commission was founded in 1973 at David Rockefeller's insistence. By 1980, 21 former members held posts in the Carter administration, including Carter, Mondale, Brzezinski and Defense Secretary Harold Brown.

channels.n: CFR War and Peace Studies: New York → State Department
channels.d: During the Second World War the council's confidential War and Peace Studies group, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, wrote 682 classified memoranda for the State Department.

channels.n: Young Global Leaders → heads of government: Cologny → Ottawa / Paris / Wellington / Helsinki
channels.d: Alumni of the WEF's Young Global Leaders programme who later led governments include Justin Trudeau (Canada), Emmanuel Macron (France), Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand) and Sanna Marin (Finland).

channels.n: Mont Pelerin members in office: Mont Pèlerin → Bonn / Rome / Prague / Santiago / Colombo
channels.d: Society members who held top office include Ludwig Erhard (West German economics minister and chancellor), Luigi Einaudi (President of Italy), Václav Klaus (Czech president), Carlos Cáceres (Chilean finance minister) and Ranil Wickremesinghe (Sri Lankan prime minister).

channels.n: Stand Your Ground: Tallahassee → ALEC model bill (Arlington) → ~30 states
channels.d: Florida passed its Stand Your Ground law in 2005; ALEC then adopted a model bill with the same wording, and similar laws spread to about 30 states with ALEC's support.

channels.n: BCCI: Luxembourg → London → Washington (First American Bankshares)
channels.d: BCCI, registered in Luxembourg and run from London and Karachi, secretly controlled Washington's First American Bankshares through nominee investors; Clark Clifford was its chairman. The Kerry–Brown Senate report found Clifford and Robert Altman closely involved with BCCI from 1978 to 1991.
channels.cite: Kerry–Brown report to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 1992

channels.n: BCCI: London → Panama City (Noriega accounts)
channels.d: BCCI was accused of laundering money for Panama's Manuel Noriega; bankers Amjad Awan and Syed Hussain reportedly managed his accounts.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → London (Christine Lee alert, 2022)
channels.d: In January 2022 MI5 issued an interference alert to MPs naming solicitor Christine Lee as suspected of acting for the United Front Work Department.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → Ottawa / Vancouver (Canada)
channels.d: A February 2022 Canadian court ruling found the UFWD's Overseas Chinese Affairs Office engaged in covert intelligence gathering; a Privy Council Office warning described Chinese interference as likely to be persistent and pervasive.

channels.n: United Front: Beijing → New York (Liang Litang indictment, 2023)
channels.d: The US sanctioned UFWD head You Quan in January 2021, and in May 2023 indicted Liang Litang as an illegal agent; senators asked the Justice Department to investigate 'Overseas Chinese Service Centers' in seven cities.
channels.cite: US Treasury sanctions 2021; US DOJ indictment 2023

channels.n: Chinese-linked donors: Beijing → Sydney / Canberra (Dastyari, 2016–17)
channels.d: A Chinese company with government links paid $44,000 of Senator Sam Dastyari's legal bills in 2014; he later took positions at odds with Australia's South China Sea policy and warned donor Huang Xiangmo his phones were likely tapped. He announced his resignation on 12 December 2017.

channels.n: Susurluk: Ankara → Susurluk crash (1996)
channels.d: Grey Wolves second-in-command Abdullah Çatlı died in the November 1996 Susurluk car crash; the scandal exposed ties between the group, the Counter-Guerrilla and state officials.

channels.n: Black Hand: Belgrade → Sarajevo (1914)
channels.d: Apis allegedly decided to have Archduke Franz Ferdinand killed; three young Bosnian Serbs were recruited, trained and smuggled from Serbia into Bosnia. The assassination on 28 June 1914 helped set off the July Crisis.

channels.n: Aum Shinrikyo: Tokyo → Moscow → Podgorica
channels.d: Aum built a Russian following; a 2000 plot to free Asahara involved a Russian member. Russia opened a criminal case and banned the group in 2016, the same year Montenegro expelled 58 foreigners linked to it.

channels.n: The Fellowship: Washington → Kampala (prayer breakfast)
channels.d: Journalist Jeff Sharlet tied Fellowship associates to Uganda's proposed anti-gay bill with a death penalty, which a member denied. In 2023 the Fellowship paid for a US congressman's keynote at Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast.

channels.n: The Fellowship: Moscow → Washington (Butina, 2017)
channels.d: Maria Butina, who later admitted acting as an undeclared Kremlin agent, helped arrange Russian attendance at the 2017 National Prayer Breakfast; the FBI interviewed organiser Doug Burleigh about her.

channels.n: TFP spread: São Paulo → Buenos Aires / Santiago / Montevideo (1967) → Warsaw
channels.d: From the Brazilian TFP (1960), national TFPs were founded in Argentina, Chile and Uruguay in 1967 and in Poland in 1995; Poland's Ordo Iuris was founded in 2013 by the TFP-linked Christian Culture Association.

channels.n: El Yunque: Puebla → Madrid (HazteOír)
channels.d: Álvaro Delgado linked El Yunque to Spain's HazteOír and CitizenGo; in 2014 a Madrid judge said evidence possibly showed links between HazteOír members and El Yunque but could not confirm the organisation exists.

channels.n: Sangh overseas: Nagpur → Nairobi (1947) → London
channels.d: The RSS's overseas wing began in Nairobi on 14 January 1947 as the Bharatiya Swayamsevak Sangh, later the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh, with branches in Kenya, the UK, Australia and Nepal.

channels.n: NXIVM: Albany → Mexico City / Vancouver
channels.d: NXIVM ran centres in Mexico and Canada as well as the US; Emiliano Salinas, son of former president Carlos Salinas, and Ana Cristina Fox, daughter of Vicente Fox, have been accused of involvement, and the Vancouver chapter recruited actresses including Allison Mack.

channels.n: Kingdom of Jesus Christ: Davao → California / Hawaii
channels.d: A US grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for child sex trafficking and misuse of church donations; FBI raids hit church sites in California, Texas and Hawaii.

channels.n: Gulen-linked teachers removed or targeted for removal to Turkey, 2017–2021
channels.d: Malaysia deported three Turks to Turkey on 11 May 2017; an attempt to fly Veysel Akcay out of Ulaanbaatar was stopped on 27 July 2018 when Mongolian authorities grounded the plane; Orhan Inandi was taken from Bishkek to Turkey in mid-2021, which Erdogan announced on 5 July 2021.
channels.cite: Al Jazeera 12 May 2017; Euronews 28 July 2018; 24.kg 17 August 2021

channels.n: Gulen schools handed to Turkey's Maarif Foundation — Pakistan
channels.d: Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered on 28 December 2018 that Pak-Turk schools be transferred to the Turkiye Maarif Foundation.

channels.n: Moon group money into Uruguay's Banco de Crédito, 1981–2002
channels.d: Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito in 1981; Uruguay's parliamentary banking commission found the bank lent about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies before it closed in 2002.

channels.n: Taizhou Taiwan Affairs Office tours for Chiayi village chiefs, 2023
channels.d: The Taizhou Taiwan Affairs Office paid lodging and local travel for Chiayi village and ward chiefs on 2023 trips organised by Lin Hsueh-feng, convicted 28 May 2025.

channels.n: CIA money to the Congress for Cultural Freedom
channels.d: The CIA's International Organizations Division paid for the Paris secretariat, which subsidised magazines and national committees in about 35 countries until 1966-67.

channels.n: CIA via Free Trade Union Committee to European unions
channels.d: CIA money passed through the AFL's Free Trade Union Committee to Irving Brown in Paris and on to Force Ouvrière, Italian unions and port groups.

channels.n: USAID and AIFLD to Brazilian union trainees
channels.d: USAID contracts funded AIFLD's training institutes in Brazil, whose graduates its director said took part in the 1964 conspiracy.

channels.n: CIA to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
places: National Committee for a Free Europe, New York
channels.d: Covert CIA funds flowed through the New York committee to the Munich stations, which broadcast into the Soviet bloc until open funding began in 1971-74.

channels.n: Ford Foundation: Jakarta to Berkeley and back to the cabinet
channels.d: Ford grants sent University of Indonesia economists to Berkeley; they returned to run BAPPENAS and the finance ministry from 1967-68.

channels.n: US aid: Santiago to Chicago and back to the junta
channels.d: US aid, then Ford money, paid for 126 Chilean economists to train at Chicago in 1955-73; from 1975 they held Pinochet's economic ministries.

channels.n: Saudi trust account through the US Treasury
channels.d: Saudi money deposited in a US Treasury trust account paid for US technical staff placed in Saudi agencies under the 1974 Joint Commission.

channels.n: Red Notice requests from member governments to Lyon
channels.d: Governments file notices with the General Secretariat in Lyon; notices later found political were refused or deleted, sometimes after arrests abroad.

channels.n: Rio 2016 vote payment to an IOC member
channels.d: Brazilian prosecutors say $2 million was routed through businessman Arthur Soares to Lamine Diack before the IOC chose Rio in Copenhagen in October 2009.

channels.n: Tobacco companies to WHO through partners
channels.d: The Zeltner Committee traced tobacco-company work through consultants, food subsidiaries and other UN bodies aimed at WHO tobacco control.

channels.n: NED grants to Venezuela's Cedice
channels.d: From 1998 NED's business institute CIPE made regular grants to Cedice, Atlas's Caracas think tank, whose director signed the 2002 Carmona Decree.

channels.n: Milner's Kindergarten: London → Cape Town / Johannesburg, 1901–1910
channels.d: Milner brought Oxford graduates from London into the Cape High Commission and the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations (1901–05); most returned to London in 1909–10 after the Union, while Duncan and Feetham stayed in South Africa.

channels.n: Round Table groups: London → dominion capitals, 1909–1915
channels.d: Lionel Curtis toured the dominions in 1910–11 setting up local Round Table groups (Canada, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand; Newfoundland 1912). Quigley adds India and a loose US group by 1915. City placement for each dominion group is approximate.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Round Table movement'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 950

channels.n: Hotel Majestic, Paris 1919 → Chatham House (London) and CFR (New York)
channels.d: On 30 May 1919 British and American delegation experts at the Hotel Majestic proposed an Anglo-American institute; the British side founded Chatham House (1920) and the American side merged with a New York group to form the Council on Foreign Relations (1921). Quigley says Chatham House treated the CFR as its American branch.
channels.cite: Chatham House (2019); CFR centennial history (2021); Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 182–191

channels.n: Chatham House → dominion institutes of international affairs, 1927 onward
channels.d: Quigley writes that Chatham House set up branch institutes in each dominion, each formed around the local Round Table members, the earliest in Canada and Australia in 1927, with the question taken up at the 1933 Toronto Commonwealth relations conference. Dates for each institute are not verified here.
channels.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10, p. 191

channels.n: Morgan–Lazard axis: New York ↔ London
channels.d: Quigley describes the 'chief backbone' of the network as financial cooperation between the Morgan bank in New York and London financiers led by Lazard Brothers and Morgan, Grenfell; he says Milner refused a Morgan partnership in London in 1901 and that Brand and then Adam Marris were managing directors of Lazard. This is Quigley's account.

channels.n: Institute of Pacific Relations conference circuit, 1925–1936
channels.d: IPR conferences met at Honolulu (1925, 1927), Kyoto (1929), Shanghai (1931), Banff (1933) and Yosemite (1936). Quigley says the British and dominion delegations were drawn from the same Milner Group circles as the Commonwealth relations conferences.
channels.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10; Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'

channels.n: Pilgrims Society: London ↔ New York, 1902–03
channels.d: The London society (1902) and New York society (1903) hold reciprocal membership and welcome each other's ambassadors.

channels.n: UAE–Amdjarass–Darfur supply route to the RSF (UN panel)
channels.d: A UN Panel of Experts report leaked in January 2024 found 'credible' evidence that the UAE flew weapons to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces several times a week through the airstrip at Amdjarass in northern Chad, from where supplies crossed into Darfur. The UAE says its 122 flights carried humanitarian aid.
channels.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Sudan (Jan 2024), reported by Al Jazeera

channels.n: Russian military air bridge Syria–eastern Libya for Wagner
channels.d: UN monitors and US Africa Command reported Russian military flights from Syria to eastern Libya supplying Wagner and Haftar's forces in 2019–20, including 338 flights counted in one UN report and Syrian fighters recruited by Wagner flown in on at least 33 Cham Wings flights. Russia later used eastern Libyan bases as logistics hubs for Africa Corps.
channels.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya; AFRICOM, as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Gupta money route: South African state contracts to Dubai
channels.d: The leaked #GuptaLeaks emails showed funds from the Free State government's Vrede dairy project laundered through Dubai paid for the family's 2013 Sun City wedding. A South African Council of Churches and academics' report estimated about R40 billion moved to Dubai from state-company deals in 2011–2017. The family moved to Dubai in 2016.
channels.cite: News24 #GuptaLeaks (2017); SACC report (2017), as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Chinese police outposts in the Americas
channels.d: Outposts that Safeguard Defenders attributed to the Fuzhou city and Qingtian county police. The Manhattan site led to US convictions (2024, 2026); the RCMP closed its Quebec probe in 2025 without charges; no Latin American government has reported findings.
channels.cite: Safeguard Defenders reports, 2022; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

channels.n: Indian intelligence plots against Sikh activists in North America
channels.d: Canada linked agents of India's government to the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar and expelled six diplomats; US prosecutors charged RAW officer Vikash Yadav with directing a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York and said he sent video of Nijjar's body to the go-between.
channels.cite: Government of Canada, October 2024; US v. Yadav and Gupta (S.D.N.Y.)

channels.n: Egypt and Qatar to Senator Menendez
channels.d: Prosecutors showed bribes flowing to Senator Menendez in return for help to the Egyptian government and for favourable words about Qatar to secure Qatari royal investment for a New Jersey developer; convicted 16 July 2024.

channels.n: Russian Interior Ministry police training in Central America
channels.d: Russia's Interior Ministry runs a police training centre in Managua for Nicaraguan and regional officers; the US Treasury sanctioned it on 15 May 2024.

channels.n: China's Ministry of Public Security police cooperation in the Pacific
channels.d: China's Ministry of Public Security has embedded officers in Fiji's police (2013–2024), sent advisory teams to the Solomon Islands (from 2022), Kiribati and Vanuatu (from 2023), and supplied equipment and training in China.
channels.cite: East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024; RFA/BenarNews, 20 March 2024

channels.n: Prince Group assets seized across Asia and London
channels.d: After the US and UK acted against Chen Zhi on 14 October 2025, the UK froze 19 London properties, Singapore seized S$150 million, Taiwan seized NT$4.5 billion and Hong Kong HK$2.75 billion.
channels.cite: US DOJ / UK sanctions, October 2025, as summarised on Wikipedia

channels.n: Fuzhou and Qingtian police bureaus to European 'service stations'
channels.d: Safeguard Defenders listed stations run for the Fuzhou city police in Dublin, Prato, Budapest, Paris, Prague and Athens, among others.

channels.n: Qingtian county police to stations in Rome, Milan, Florence, Vienna, Frankfurt
channels.d: Stations listed for the Qingtian County Public Security Bureau, a home county of many Chinese migrants in Italy and Austria.

channels.n: Baku to PACE Strasbourg and Milan — caviar diplomacy payments
channels.d: Money from Azerbaijan-linked companies reached PACE members, including €2.39 million to Italian Luca Volontè (convicted in Milan, 2021) and payments to German members whose immunity the Bundestag lifted in 2021.
channels.cite: PACE Independent Investigation Body 2018; Court of Milan 2021

channels.n: Azerbaijani Laundromat — Baku through Danske Bank Tallinn
channels.d: About $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 from Azerbaijani sources through four UK-registered shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

channels.n: Doha and Rabat to Brussels — Qatargate cash
channels.d: Belgian investigators say cash from Qatar and Morocco reached the European Parliament through former MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri and his NGO Fight Impunity.

channels.n: Moscow to Paris — Front National bank loan
channels.d: €9 million loan from the First Czech Russian Bank to the Front National, 2014.

channels.n: Moscow Metropol to Milan — Lega oil-deal talks
channels.d: October 2018 Metropol hotel meeting on an oil deal meant to finance the Lega; case dismissed in 2023.

channels.n: Medvedchuk network — Prague hub to European parliaments
channels.d: Voice of Europe was run from Prague and used Belgium as a hub for meetings and payments; German prosecutors in Munich investigate an MEP; in London, Nathan Gill was convicted of taking bribes passed on for Medvedchuk.
channels.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; Old Bailey 2025

channels.n: Ankara to Pristina and Chișinău — renditions of Gülen-linked teachers
channels.d: Six Turks were flown from Kosovo to Turkey in March 2018 and seven teachers from Moldova in September 2018; Kosovo's spy chief was later convicted and the European Court of Human Rights ruled against Moldova.
channels.cite: Basic Court of Pristina 2023; ECtHR Ozdil and Others v. Moldova 2019

channels.n: Ankara Diyanet to DITIB Cologne
channels.d: DITIB's imams are trained in Ankara and paid as Turkish civil servants by the Diyanet.

channels.n: Odebrecht bribery network across Latin America and Africa
channels.d: In its December 2016 plea agreement Odebrecht admitted paying $788 million in bribes in 12 countries between 2001 and 2016 through its Structured Operations Division.

channels.n: Glencore bribes paid in five African states (UK SFO case)
channels.d: The UK Serious Fraud Office found more than $28 million in bribes paid by Glencore's UK oil arm in Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan in 2012–2016.
channels.cite: UK SFO, Southwark Crown Court, June 2022

channels.n: Erik Prince's security deals with governments, 2019–2026
channels.d: A UN panel found Prince broke the Libya arms embargo in 2019; in 2025–26 he made security deals with Ecuador's president, ran anti-gang operations in Haiti through Vectus Global, and sent men and drones to help Congo's army at Uvira.
channels.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya, Feb 2021; Reuters 2025–26

channels.n: Unification Church honours and fees to heads of government
channels.d: From its Seoul headquarters the Unification Church, through the Universal Peace Federation and the Sunhak Peace Prize, gave a governance award to Cambodia's sitting prime minister (2019), a US$1 million-class peace prize to Senegal's sitting president (2020) and speaking fees of $2–2.5 million to Donald Trump (2021–22).

channels.n: Diyanet imam network in Western Europe
channels.d: Turkey's Diyanet sends state-employed imams to mosques run by its branches abroad. Germany investigated DITIB imams for spying (2017), Austria reviewed the permits of about 40 ATIB imams (2018), a Dutch parliamentary inquiry found strong Diyanet political influence (2020), and Belgian State Security found a Diyanet employee in the new Brussels mosque body (2020).
channels.cite: Politico Europe 2017; Al Jazeera 2018; DutchNews 2020; Belgian Justice Ministry 2020

channels.n: Gulf Salafi funding to Belgian and Dutch mosques
channels.d: The Muslim World League ran the Great Mosque of Brussels for Saudi Arabia until Belgium ended the lease in 2018; the 2020 Dutch parliamentary inquiry traced Salafi mosque funding to donors in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar.

channels.n: Moscow Patriarchate churches cut off by neighbouring states
channels.d: After the 2022 invasion, Latvia (2022), Estonia (2024) and Ukraine (2024) used laws, residence permits and bans to sever local Orthodox churches from the Moscow Patriarchate.
channels.cite: Wikipedia articles on the Latvian, Estonian and Ukrainian churches; ERR News

channels.n: Universal Church from Brazil to Angola
channels.d: The UCKG's Brazilian leadership placed bishops in Brazil's Congress, cabinet and Rio City Hall, and ran the church in Angola until the Angolan government removed its Brazilian leaders in 2020.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God'

channels.n: US Christian lobbies and Uganda's anti-gay laws
channels.d: Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that David Bahati, chair of Uganda's Fellowship-linked National Prayer Breakfast, floated his 2009 bill at the 2008 breakfast; an activist named Family Watch International's president as a lobbyist for the 2023 Act.

channels.n: Crypto AG: Swiss machines, readers in Langley and Pullach
channels.d: Cipher machines made in Zug were sold to governments in more than 120 countries while the CIA (Langley) and BND (Pullach) owned the firm and read the traffic.

channels.n: Marsalek network: Moscow to Munich, Vienna and London
channels.d: Former Wirecard COO Jan Marsalek, now in Russia, directed a Bulgarian spy cell in London and took material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott.

channels.n: North Korean IT workers: China border to US laptop farms
channels.d: Kejia Wang met a North Korean contact in Shenyang and Dandong and ran US laptop farms; Christina Chapman ran another in Arizona. Workers abroad logged in through the farms to US company networks.

channels.n: Russian money through Moldovan courts to Latvian banks (Global Laundromat)
channels.d: Russian firms 'guaranteed' fake debts, Moldovan judges ordered them paid into Moldindconbank, and the money moved on through Latvian banks to shell companies, many registered in the UK, in 2010–14.
channels.cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta, Global Laundromat

channels.n: Calabrian and Sicilian betting money through Malta licences
channels.d: Italian investigations found mafia groups collecting bets in Italy through companies licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority, hiding ownership behind fiduciaries.

channels.n: Casamance rosewood through Banjul to China
channels.d: Rosewood logged in Senegal's Casamance was trucked into The Gambia and shipped from Banjul; The Gambia exported about $163 million to China in 2014–17.
channels.cite: TRIAL International (2019); EIA 'Cashing in on Chaos' (2020)

channels.n: Kokang scam bosses handed from Laukkai to Chinese courts
channels.d: Myanmar handed Kokang family leaders to China in 2023–24; the Bai group was tried in Shenzhen and the Ming family in Wenzhou, and members of both were executed in early 2026.

channels.n: Rotterdam cocaine fugitive to Freetown
channels.d: Dutch police believed Jos Leijdekkers lived in Turkey before Reuters placed him in Sierra Leone in 2025.

channels.n: Rothschild five-house network
channels.d: Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons set up cooperating houses in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples, which moved government money across Europe, including British war subsidies before 1815.
channels.cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope p. 51; Wikipedia 'Rothschild family'

channels.n: Morgan axis: 23 Wall Street–Morgan, Grenfell–Morgan, Harjes
channels.d: J.P. Morgan & Co. worked with its London affiliate (J.S. Morgan & Co., later Morgan, Grenfell) and Paris affiliate (Morgan, Harjes); in 1914–17 this axis handled British and French war purchasing and loans in the US. Quigley calls the New York–London tie to Lazard Brothers 'the chief backbone' of the Round Table organisation.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan', 'American entry into World War I'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope p. 951

channels.n: Jekyll Island to the Federal Reserve Board
channels.d: New York bankers from Morgan, National City and Kuhn, Loeb travelled with Senator Aldrich to Jekyll Island in November 1910 to draft the Aldrich Plan; the Federal Reserve Act followed in 1913 and Paul Warburg joined the Board in Washington in 1914.
channels.cite: Federal Reserve History, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island'

channels.n: Goldman Sachs to treasuries and central banks
channels.d: Former Goldman Sachs partners and staff moved into the US Treasury and White House (Rubin, Paulson, Cohn), the Bank of Italy, ECB and Italian premiership (Draghi, Monti), the Bank of Canada, Bank of England and Canadian premiership (Carney) and the German finance ministry (Kukies).
channels.cite: Wikipedia biographies of Rubin, Paulson, Cohn, Draghi, Monti, Carney, Kukies

channels.n: Basel: central bank governors' meetings
channels.d: Governors of the main central banks have met privately in Basel since 1930, monthly in the 1930s and every two months since 1998; Quigley described this as the apex of a world system of financial control.
channels.cite: Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope p. 324

channels.n: Lazard London to wartime Washington
channels.d: Quigley traces Lazard Brothers men (Robert Brand, Thomas Brand, Adam Marris) into Britain's wartime missions and embassy in Washington, 1940–46.

channels.n: Schiff's Japanese war loans
channels.d: Jacob Schiff met Bank of Japan deputy governor Takahashi Korekiyo in Paris in April 1904 and floated about $200 million of Japanese war bonds in New York.

channels.n: Credit Suisse–Privinvest–Maputo tuna-bond loans
channels.d: Loans arranged by Credit Suisse bankers in London went to Mozambican state companies for Privinvest contracts; kickbacks flowed back to the bankers through UAE companies.

channels.n: NSA access to Danish cables used to spy on European leaders (2012–14)
channels.d: Per the Danish FE's 'Dunhammer' review, the NSA used Danish cable intercepts to wiretap German leaders, with reported targets in Sweden, Norway and France.

channels.n: Rigged Crypto AG machines to customer governments
channels.d: Crypto AG sold cipher machines to more than 120 governments while secretly owned by the CIA and BND; Iran is one named customer.

channels.n: UAE money to Alp Services to target Europeans (2017–21)
channels.d: At least €5.7m paid via an Emirati front to Alp, which compiled files on people in 18 European countries, with the largest counts in Belgium, Italy and Norway.
